query:
Please rubber-duck (critique, with sources) the beam delivery of a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion machine for aluminium alloys. Beam path: a 500 W single-mode CW Yb fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500-U3-SM-AC, M2 1.05-1.1, QBH-compatible output, 5 m fibre) into IPG's standard collimator (5 mm or 7.5 mm collimated beam), then a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (20 mm aperture, mirrors rated about 1 kW at 1064 nm without cooling), then a fused-silica f-theta lens with f = 160 mm (Thorlabs FTH160-1064 class) or f = 254 mm, then an AR-coated fused-silica chamber window (Thorlabs WG41050-C class, 2 in.) with a replaceable 3 mm fused-silica cover slide below it, then a 25-75 mm diameter heated (200 C) build plate in argon at +5 to +20 mbar with a cross-flow of 2.5-3 m/s. Target spot ~75 um (1/e2), layer 30-60 um, powder AlSi10Mg and Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, some Mg- and Zn-bearing alloys.

Questions: (1) Thermal focal shift: how much focal shift do fused-silica collimators, f-theta lenses and windows show at 300-500 W CW single-mode with clean and with contaminated (soot, condensate) surfaces, and how do LPBF machines detect or compensate it (Z-scan burn tests, focus monitoring)? (2) Is a low-cost f-theta lens (Thorlabs FTH series, EKSMA, Wavelength Opto, Sill, Ronar-Smith) suitable at 500 W CW, given coating absorption and damage thresholds? What do commercial LPBF machines use (Sill, Linos/Excelitas, Ronar-Smith; telecentric or not)? (3) Back-reflection from aluminium melt pools into a single-mode fibre laser: how much power returns through a galvo and f-theta, what damage does it cause, how do LPBF builders protect the laser (isolators, tilting the window, keeping the scan field off-axis, the laser's own back-reflection protection)? (4) Window and cover-slide contamination by Mg/Zn vapour condensate and spatter: deposition rates, effect on transmitted power, how often slides are changed, purge designs that keep the window clean, and whether to tilt the window to avoid ghost reflections into the beam path. (5) Galvo aperture clipping and mirror heating: what beam diameter margin to keep for a 20 mm aperture, angle of incidence on the powder bed at the edge of a 75 mm field with f = 160 mm and its effect on spot ellipticity and absorption. (6) What optical instruments are needed to commission and calibrate such a system (power meter able to take 500 W, beam profiler or focus finder, IR viewer, alignment laser, scan-field calibration plates), and what melt-pool monitoring (coaxial photodiode via a dichroic, off-axis camera, pyrometer) fits a basiCube-class head? (7) Laser safety optics: which window materials and OD ratings for viewing windows in a Class 1 enclosure, and guard burn-through times for 1.6 mm aluminium at 500 W. Please give numbers with sources.
task_summary: Beam Delivery Assessment For 500W Single Mode LPBF Including Thermal Focal Shift Optics Suitability

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->

target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->

List of drug names to generate or filter results.

drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Please rubber-duck (critique, with sources) the beam delivery of a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion machine for aluminium alloys. Beam path: a 500 W single-mode CW Yb fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500-U3-SM-AC, M2 1.05-1.1, QBH-compatible output, 5 m fibre) into IPG's standard collimator (5 mm or 7.5 mm collimated beam), then a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (20 mm aperture, mirrors rated about 1 kW at 1064 nm without cooling), then a fused-silica f-theta lens with f = 160 mm (Thorlabs FTH160-1064 class) or f = 254 mm, then an AR-coated fused-silica chamber window (Thorlabs WG41050-C class, 2 in.) with a replaceable 3 mm fused-silica cover slide below it, then a 25-75 mm diameter heated (200 C) build plate in argon at +5 to +20 mbar with a cross-flow of 2.5-3 m/s. Target spot ~75 um (1/e2), layer 30-60 um, powder AlSi10Mg and Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, some Mg- and Zn-bearing alloys.

Questions: (1) Thermal focal shift: how much focal shift do fused-silica collimators, f-theta lenses and windows show at 300-500 W CW single-mode with clean and with contaminated (soot, condensate) surfaces, and how do LPBF machines detect or compensate it (Z-scan burn tests, focus monitoring)? (2) Is a low-cost f-theta lens (Thorlabs FTH series, EKSMA, Wavelength Opto, Sill, Ronar-Smith) suitable at 500 W CW, given coating absorption and damage thresholds? What do commercial LPBF machines use (Sill, Linos/Excelitas, Ronar-Smith; telecentric or not)? (3) Back-reflection from aluminium melt pools into a single-mode fibre laser: how much power returns through a galvo and f-theta, what damage does it cause, how do LPBF builders protect the laser (isolators, tilting the window, keeping the scan field off-axis, the laser's own back-reflection protection)? (4) Window and cover-slide contamination by Mg/Zn vapour condensate and spatter: deposition rates, effect on transmitted power, how often slides are changed, purge designs that keep the window clean, and whether to tilt the window to avoid ghost reflections into the beam path. (5) Galvo aperture clipping and mirror heating: what beam diameter margin to keep for a 20 mm aperture, angle of incidence on the powder bed at the edge of a 75 mm field with f = 160 mm and its effect on spot ellipticity and absorption. (6) What optical instruments are needed to commission and calibrate such a system (power meter able to take 500 W, beam profiler or focus finder, IR viewer, alignment laser, scan-field calibration plates), and what melt-pool monitoring (coaxial photodiode via a dichroic, off-axis camera, pyrometer) fits a basiCube-class head? (7) Laser safety optics: which window materials and OD ratings for viewing windows in a Class 1 enclosure, and guard burn-through times for 1.6 mm aluminium at 500 W. Please give numbers with sources.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
Abstract. Non-uniform (gradient) heating due to absorption of laser radiation in optical elements causes thermal lensing and paraxial focus shift and aberration leading to change in size and intensity profile of focused spot in optics operating with high-power lasers. Analysis of primary physical effects of geometrical deformation of optical surfaces in the form of aspheric bulges and transformation of the material into a gradient refractive medium makes it possible to estimate quantitatively the focus shift and aberrations for single-mode and multimode lasers, to formulate optimal relationships between the physical properties of optical materials for reduction of thermo-optical effects through compensating the effects from material thermal expansion by the effects due to change in the refractive index—condition of self-compensation or athermalization. Comparison of characteristics Temperature Coefficient of the Optical Pathlength and Thermo-Optical Ratio allows determining the optimal materials for the optics for high-power lasers: athermal crystalline quartz and specialty glasses, sapphire with extremely high thermal conductivity ensuring minimal temperature gradients. Optics made of these materials exhibit minimized thermal focus shift and aberration even when absorption of laser energy in bulk material and coatings, by contamination, scratches, and other surface defects. Weak birefringence of crystalline quartz and sapphire does not prevent their successive use in laser optics.

Abstract:
This paper describes the development of suitable process parameters to ensure a reproducible, defect-free production of pure copper specimen via Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) also called Selective Laser Melting (SLM). Therefore, a set of experiments was developed and evaluated in a Design of Experiment (DoE) which finally provide an indication about ideal process parameters for melting pure copper powder at a wavelength of 1064 nm. For the experiments Cu-ETP with a copper purity of more than 99.90 % was processed with a laser power of up to 500 W resulting in a maximum density of 99.82 % and an electrical conductivity of 56.88 MS/m. Besides the development of optimal parameter combinations of laser power, laser speed and hatching distance, focusing the laser beam to a spot diameter of about 35 μm with a fused silica f-theta lens and thus high energy intensities of about 416 kW/mm2 resulted in best materials properties.

Abstract:
Thermal lensing is a well-known but undesired effect in high power laser optics for welding, 3D-printing and other technologies. Stability and performance of laser processing depend on the possibility to control and minimize the thermo-optical effects induced by non-uniform (gradient) heating due to absorption of laser energy in optical elements: paraxial focus shift and thermally induced aberration, which lead to a change in size and intensity profile of the focal spot. Analysis of primary physical effects: geometrical deformation of optical surfaces and the material transformation into a gradient refractive medium, allows the quantitative estimation of the wavefront beam distortion leading to focus shift and aberration. It also allows formulating an optimal relationship between the physical properties of optical materials to reduce the change in the wavefront through mutual compensation of thermo-optical effects induced by the thermal expansion and the refractive index change – athermalization condition. Athermal optics exhibit minimized thermal focus shift and aberration even when absorbing laser energy in the bulk material and coatings, by contamination or scratches. Considering physical characteristics the Temperature Coefficient of the Optical Pathlength and ThermoOptical Ratio allows determining the optimal materials for optics: athermal crystalline Quartz and specialty glasses, Sapphire with high thermal conductivity. Weak birefringence of Quartz and Sapphire doesn’t prevent their successive use in laser optics. The comparison of the theoretical analysis and experimental validation results of optics made of Fused Silica, N-BK7, crystalline Quartz and Sapphire confirm the theoretical method for reducing the thermal focus shift and effectiveness of the suggested approach.

Abstract:
The continuous increase of the average laser power of ultrafast lasers is a challenge with respect to the thermal load of the processing optics. The power which is absorbed in an optical element leads to a temperature increase, temperature gradients, changing refractive index and shape, and finally causes distortions of the transmitted beam. In a first-order approximation this results in a change of the focal position, which may lead to an uncon-trolled change of the laser machining process. The present study reports on investigations on the focal shift induced in thin plano-convex lenses by a high-power ultra-short pulsed laser with an average laser power of up to 525 W. The focal shift was determined for lenses made of different materials (N-BK7, fused silica) and with different coatings (un-coated, broadband coating, specific wavelength coating).

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Demand for complex, application-specific optics requires processes that deliver high surface quality and figure accuracy at reduced cost and lead time. This work investigates laser beam figuring (LBF) as a deterministic, laser-based step in an integrated manufacturing chain for fused silica optics. LBF uses spatially selective CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    -laser irradiation to remove material in the nanometer range according to the difference between the actual and target surface geometry. Pulse-duration modulation enables precise depth control while maintaining low surface roughness. Building on previous studies, we address two critical gaps in the state-of-the-art. First, we experimentally determine the long-term stability of laser-induced densified regions over an unprecedented 80-week observation period, demonstrating statistically robust process stability essential for industrial applications. Second, we systematically map the transition from densification-dominated regimes (< 10 nm) to true ablation, identifying optimal process windows (dx = 10 μm, dy = 30 μm) that enable reproducible nanometer-scale figure correction with area rates competitive to conventional methods. Figure error correction experiments demonstrate RMS reduction from 79.2 nm to 30.6 nm in a single pass. However, LBF introduces high-frequency surface features (λ < 100 μm), suggesting integration with chemo-mechanical post-polishing for applications requiring ultra-smooth surfaces. The results provide a quantitative foundation for LBF as a complementary technology to ion beam figuring and magnetorheological finishing, particularly suited for rapid prototyping and laser-based process chains.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Due to the rapid development of precision manufacturing technology, much research has been conducted in the field of multisensor measurement and data fusion technology with a goal of enhancing monitoring capabilities in terms of measurement accuracy and information richness, thereby improving the efficiency and precision of manufacturing. In a multisensor system, each sensor independently measures certain parameters. Then, the system uses a relevant signal-processing algorithm to combine all of the independent measurements into a comprehensive set of measurement results. The purpose of this paper is to describe multisensor measurement and data fusion technology and its applications in precision monitoring systems. The architecture of multisensor measurement systems is reviewed, and some implementations in manufacturing systems are presented. In addition to the multisensor measurement system, related data fusion methods and algorithms are summarized. Further perspectives on multisensor monitoring and data fusion technology are included at the end of this paper.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Copper possesses exceptional thermal and electrical conductivity, making it valuable in applications ranging from electronics and heat exchangers to aerospace and energy systems. However, its high reflectivity, thermal conductivity, and susceptibility to oxidation present significant challenges in laser additive manufacturing (AM). This review presents a comprehensive overview of the current state of laser AM of copper and copper alloys, with a focus on laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and laser directed energy deposition (LDED) techniques. The key processing challenges are outlined, including limited laser absorption with infrared lasers, melt pool instability, and porosity formation. Strategies to enhance the processability of copper and its alloys are critically reviewed, including process parameter optimization, material modifications, and the use of alternative laser sources such as green and blue lasers. The role of process monitoring is also discussed as a pathway to ensure process stability and repeatability. The review further highlights recent applications of copper AM and identifies the transition from density-driven optimization to function-oriented qualification as a key requirement for industrial implementation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing is a vanguard production technology that has contributed greatly to speed up replacing on the market of complex-shaped components. A delicate and unavoidable phase of additive technology is that relating to the post-processing of the components, especially the finishing process. Post-processing needs to be automated and made scalable so that the technology can actually be adopted also for mass production. In this respect, an emerging post-processing technology suitable for surface finishing, not in contact and easily automatable, is the one that involves the use of laser sources, known by the name of laser polishing. Laser polishing is spreading, in fact, more and more strongly, in the field of manufacturing as a valid alternative to conventional technologies for the surface finishing of metallic components obtained by additive processes. Laser polishing is widely considered very suitable to improving the surface finish of metal components. When compared with the conventional finishing technologies, laser polishing has many benefits in terms of costs and process times especially if automated, through the use of CNC systems and scanning heads. In this manuscript, the knowledge of this technology is deepened through a review of the relevant literature that highlights the aspects of the interaction of the laser beam with the metal alloys most frequently used in 3D printing, without neglecting the importance of the thermo-mechanical properties that derive from it. The analysis conducted on the technology of laser polishing aims therefore at evaluating the potential applications in industrial engineering, mainly with regard to the surfaces quality achievable as a result of the polishing of metal components fabricated by additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
Nowadays, the use of metal processing additive technologies is a rapidly growing field in the manufacturing industry. These technologies, such as metal 3D printing (also known as additive manufacturing) and laser cladding, allow for the production of complex geometries and intricate designs that would be impossible with traditional manufacturing methods. They also offer the ability to create parts with customized properties, such as improved strength, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance. In other words, these technologies have the potential to revolutionize the way we design and produce products, reducing costs and increasing efficiency to improve product quality and functionality. One of the significant advantages of these metal processing additive technologies is a reduction in waste and environmental impact. However, there are also some challenges associated with these technologies. One of the main challenges is the cost of equipment and materials, which can be prohibitively expensive for small businesses and individuals. Additionally, the quality of parts produced with these technologies can be affected by factors such as printing speed, temperature, and post-processing methods. This review article aims to contribute to a deep understanding of the processing, properties, and applications of ferrous and non-ferrous alloys in the context of SLM to assist readers in obtaining high-quality AM components. Simultaneously, it emphasizes the importance of further research, optimization, and cost-effective approaches to promote the broader adoption of SLM technology in the industry.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT While significant progress has been made in laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) for metal additive manufacturing (AM), there is still limited large scale adoption of this advanced manufacturing technique by the industry. This paper covers the recent developments in L-PBF with discussions from the materials and process perspectives. High entropy alloys and high strength aluminium alloys have been identified as key materials development for L-PBF. Then, scanning strategies and multi-lasers applications for the process are also discussed. Other research trends and topics such as powder recycling, shape memory alloys and magnetic alloys are illustrated. The final part of this paper provides an outlook on the recent advancements while suggesting potential research topics for L-PBF.

Abstract:
Magnesium-based materials are used primarily in developing lightweight structures owing to their lower density. Further, being biocompatible they offer potential for use as bioresorbable materials for degradable bone replacement implants. The design and manufacture of complex shaped components made of magnesium with good quality are in high demand in the automotive, aerospace, and biomedical areas. Selective laser melting (SLM) is becoming a powerful additive manufacturing technology, enabling the manufacture of customized, complex metallic designs. This article reviews the recent progress in the SLM of magnesium based materials. Effects of SLM process parameters and powder properties on the processing and densification of the magnesium alloys are discussed in detail. Abstract:
Spatter during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) can induce surface defects, impacting the fatigue performance of the fabricated components. Here, we reveal and explain the links between vapour depression shape and spatter dynamics during LPBF of an Al-Fe-Zr aluminium alloy using high-speed synchrotron x-ray imaging. We quantify the number, trajectory angle, velocity, and kinetic energy of the spatter as a function of vapour depression zone/keyhole morphology under industry-relevant processing conditions. The depression zone/keyhole morphology was found to influence the spatter ejection angle in keyhole versus conduction melting modes: (i) the vapour-pressure driven plume in conduction mode with a quasi-semi-circular depression zone leads to backward spatter whereas; and (ii) the keyhole rear wall redirects the gas/vapour flow to cause vertical spatter ejection and rear rim droplet spatter. Increasing the opening of the keyhole or vapour depression zone can reduce entrainment of solid spatter. We discover a spatter-induced cavity mechanism in which small spatter particles are accelerated towards the powder bed after laser-spatter interaction, inducing powder denudation and cavities on the printed surface. By quantifying these laser-spatter interactions, we suggest a printing strategy for minimising defects and improving the surface quality of LPBF parts.

Abstract:

However, massive evaporation occurs during laser melting of Zn so that it becomes a critical issue to modulate laser energy input and gas shielding conditions to eliminate the negative effect of evaporation fume during the LPBF process. In this research, two numerical models were established to simulate the interaction between the scanning laser and Zn metal as well as the interaction between the shielding gas flow and the evaporation fume, respectively. The first model predicted the evaporation rate under different laser energy input by taking the effect of evaporation on the conservation of energy, momentum, and mass into consideration. Furthermore, the influence of evaporation on surface quality densification was discussed by comparing LPBF of pure Zn and a Titanium alloy. The established numerical analysis not only helps to find the adequate laser energy input and the optimized shielding gas flow for the LPBF of Zn based metal, but is also beneficial to understand the influence of evaporation on the LPBF process.

Abstract:
The goal of this work is to detect the onset of material cross-contamination in laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing (AM) process using data from in situ sensors. Material cross-contamination refers to trace foreign materials that may be introduced in the powder feedstock used in the process due to reasons such as poor cleaning of the machine after previous builds or inadequate quality control during production and storage of the powder. Material cross-contamination may lead to deleterious changes in the microstructure of the AM part and consequently affect its functional properties. Accordingly, the objective of this work is to develop and apply a spectral graph theoretic approach to detect the occurrence of material cross-contamination in real-time as the part is being built using in-process sensors. The central hypothesis is that transforming the process signals in the spectral graph domain leads to early and more accurate detection of material cross-contamination in L-PBF compared to the traditional delay-embedded Bon-Jenkins stochastic time series analysis techniques, such as autoregressive (AR) and autoregressive moving average (ARMA) modeling. To test this hypothesis, Inconel alloy 625 (UNS alloy 06625) test parts were made at Edison Welding Institute (EWI) on a custom-built L-PBF apparatus integrated with multiple sensors, including a silicon photodetector (with 300 nm to 1100 nm optical wavelength). During the process, two types of foreign contaminant materials, namely, tungsten and aluminum particulates, under varying degrees of severity were introduced. To detect cross-contamination in the part, the photodetector sensor signatures were monitored hatch-by-hatch in the form of spectral graph transform coefficients. These spectral graph coefficients are subsequently tracked on a Hotelling T2 statistical control chart. Instances of Type II statistical error, i.e., probability of failing to detect the onset of material cross-contamination, were verified against X-ray computed tomography (XCT) scans of the part to be within 5% in the case of aluminum contaminant particles. In contrast, traditional stochastic time series modeling approaches, e.g., ARMA, had corresponding Type II error exceeding 15%. Furthermore, the computation time for the spectral graph approach was found to be less than one millisecond, compared to nearly 100 ms for the traditional time series models tested.

Abstract:
Shaping or splitting of a Gaussian beam is often desired to optimise laser–material interactions, improving throughput and quality. This can be achieved holographically using liquid crystal-on-silicon spatial light modulators (LC-SLMs). Until recently, maximum exposure has been limited to circa 120 W average power with a Gaussian profile, restricting potential applications due to the non-linear (NL) phase response of the liquid crystal above this threshold. In this study, we present experimental tests of a new SLM device, demonstrating high first-order diffraction efficiency of η = 0.98 ± 0.01 at 300 W average power and a phase range Δφ > 2π at P = 383 W, an exceptional performance. The numerically calculated device temperature response with power closely matches that measured, supporting the higher power-handling capability. Surface modification of mild steel and molybdenum up to P = 350 W exposure is demonstrated when employing a single-mode (SM) fibre laser source. Exposure on mild steel with a vortex beam (m = +6) displays numerous ringed regions with varying micro-structures and clear elemental separation created by the radial heat flow. On molybdenum, with multi-spot Gaussian exposure, both MoO3 films and recrystallisation rings were observed, exposure-dependent. The step change in device capability will accelerate new applications for this LC-SLM in both subtractive and additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
Laser processing is a versatile tool that enhances smart materials for diverse industries, allowing precise changes in material properties and customization of surface characteristics. It drives the development of smart materials with adaptive properties through laser modification, utilizing photothermal reactions and functional additives for meticulous control. These laser-processed smart materials form the foundation of 4D printing that enables dynamic shape changes depending on external influences, with significant potential in the aerospace, robotics, health care, electronics, and automotive sectors, thus fostering innovation. Laser processing also advances photonics and optoelectronics, facilitating precise control over optical properties and promoting responsive device development for various applications. The application of computer-generated diffractive optical elements (DOEs) enhances laser precision, allowing for predetermined temperature distribution and showcasing substantial promise in enhancing smart material properties. This comprehensive overview explores the applications of laser technology and nanotechnology involving DOEs, underscoring their transformative potential in the realms of photonics and optoelectronics. The growing potential for further research and practical applications in this field suggests promising prospects in the near future.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) can fabricate intricate metal components but is prone to defects, such as porosity and cracks, that degrade performance. We present an in situ monitoring framework that fuses structure-borne acoustic emission (AE) and coaxial two-color pyrometry acquired synchronously at 1 MHz. Modality-specific encoders are pretrained separately, their latent representations are exported, and a lightweight feature-level fusion classifier with two binary heads predicts crack-like and porosity-like indications. Evaluation uses a held-out grouped experiment/build-machine-part split with independent Archimedes density and micro-CT ground truth. On the held-out test set, the fused model achieved F1 = 0.974 for crack-like detection and F1 = 0.987 for porosity-like detection, with AUROC = 0.998 and 0.993, respectively. Recall was 1.00 for both heads, corresponding to false-positive rates of 11.18% for crack-like and 0.945% for porosity-like indications. These results support synchronized AE-pyrometry fusion as a promising high-sensitivity in situ screening approach for LPBF. A later matched within-framework ablation campaign was also performed under stricter checkpoint-screening rules to compare AE + PY + Aux, AE + PY, AE-only, and PY-only variants under a common grouped-split protocol. Together, these results support multimodal monitoring while highlighting the need for explicit coupon/geometry-stratified reporting and for separately architecture-optimized unimodal baselines.</jats:p>

<jats:p>Reliable process monitoring is critical for advancing laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), as it provides the process information required for corrective control actions to prevent defects such as lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity. A promising approach for PBF-LB/M process monitoring is coaxial measurement of light emitted from the meltpool area. More than two hundred research studies on coaxial monitoring of the meltpool have been performed, but there is still no validated and reliable method for measuring a suitable variable that could be directly used as an input for high-resolution control of the PBF-LB/M process, enabling process parameters such as laser power and scan speed to be dynamically adjusted not only at the part level, but locally for individual micrometer-scale segments along the scan track. This work reviews existing research studies on coaxial meltpool monitoring and identifies potential future research and development directions toward a standard and reliable meltpool monitoring method. Meltpool depth is identified as a particularly promising control-relevant variable. With the ability to monitor and control meltpool depth, it is possible to avoid undesirable process conditions due to too high or too low energy input, which would result in defects like keyhole porosity or lack-of-fusion. However, only five studies have attempted to estimate the melt pool depth coaxially during the PBF-LB/M process. Despite these attempts, there is no sufficiently validated method for high-resolution coaxial monitoring of meltpool depth in PBF-LB/M. The potential solution seems to be in combining concepts and recent discoveries from two-color coaxial camera- and photodiode-based meltpool area monitoring approaches. Based on the existing literature and hands-on experiences with establishing and working with coaxial monitoring systems, this work also provides guidelines and lists the most common challenges for implementing coaxial monitoring of the meltpool in the PBF-LB/M process.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Thermal management devices such as heat exchangers and heat pipes are integral to safe and efficient performance in multiple engineering applications, including lithium-ion batteries, electric vehicles, electronics, and renewable energy. However, the functional designs of these devices have until now been created around conventional manufacturing constraints, and thermal performance has plateaued as a result. While 3D printing offers the design freedom to address these limitations, there has been a notable lack in high thermal conductivity materials beyond aluminium alloys. Recently, the 3D printing of pure copper to sufficiently high densities has finally taken off, due to the emergence of commercial-grade printers which are now equipped with 1 kW high-power lasers or short-wavelength lasers. Although the capabilities of these new systems appear ideal for processing pure copper as a bulk material, the performance of advanced thermal management devices are strongly dependent on topology-optimised filigree structures, which can require a very different processing window. Hence, this article presents a broad overview of the state-of-the-art in various additive manufacturing technologies used to fabricate pure copper functional filigree geometries comprising thin walls, lattice structures, and porous foams, and identifies opportunities for future developments in the 3D printing of pure copper for advanced thermal management devices.

Abstract : Satellite lifetime is often limited by degradation of the electrical power subsystem--radiation-damaged solar arrays and failed batteries, Being able to beam power from terrestrial sites could alleviate this limitation, extending the lifetime of billions of dollars of satellite assets, as well as providing additional energy for electric propulsion that can be used for stationkeeping and orbital changes In addition, laboratory research at the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) has shown the potential to anneal damaged solar cells using lasers, This thesis describes that research, preliminary work performed lasing a representative solar panel array, and a proposed on-orbit experiment to demonstrate the relevant concepts by lasing PAN SAT, an NPS-built and operated spacecraft, The preliminary work done at Maui involved lasing a PAN SAT silicon photovoltaic array using a 975 nm% Yb:YAG source at output power levels of 7 W, 14 W and 21 W, These results matched those obtained under near-AMO conditions atop Mount Haleakala (for the 7 W case) and extrapolated to match predicted output levels, Enough data points were collected at each power level to generate an I-V curve for the panel, identifying the open circuit voltage, short circuit current, and maximum power points, The efficiency of the panel varied from 13,1% (as expected for monochromatic light) at 7 W to 11,3% at 21 W due to uniform heating of the cells, These results represent a "ground truth" baseline from which further research can continue,

Abstract:
This review article presents a comprehensive and in-depth discussion of thermal management, optical performance enhancement, and reliability issues in semiconductor laser packaging technology. By synthesising existing literature and research results, the article presents a systematic summary of the research progress and practical applications of semiconductor laser packaging technology in these key areas. In the section on thermal management, the article reviews different heat sink technologies, packaging structures, and solid crystal materials with the aim of improving the thermal stability and long-term reliability of semiconductor la ser devices. In the section on optical performance enhancement, the article outlines beam shaping techniques and packaging technologies. It also addresses reliability issues in packaging, discussing optical mirror damage as well as stress and mechanical damage. The aim of this review is to provide assistance for the further development and application of semiconductor laser packaging technology, with the objective of promoting the rapid and healthy development of the laser industry.

Abstract:
<jats:p>With the continuous development of science and technology, aircraft structural health monitoring (SHM) has become increasingly important in the aviation field. As a key component of SHM, wing deformation monitoring is of great significance for ensuring flight safety and reducing maintenance costs. The traditional strain gauge measurement method can no longer meet the needs of modern aeronautical engineering. Fiber Bragg grating (FBG) sensors have been widely used in the engineering field due to their unique advantages, and have shown great potential in aircraft wing deformation monitoring. In the context of SHM in the aircraft field, this article provides an overview of four aspects: classification and principles of fiber optic sensors, packaging forms of FBG sensors, bonding technology, and calibration technology. The packaging forms includes tube-packaged, embedded package and surface-attached package. It then discuss the bonding technology of FBG sensors, and the principle and influencing factors of fiber optic bonding technology are analyzed. Finally, it conducts in-depth research on the calibration technology of FBG sensors. Through comprehensive analysis of these four aspects, the suggestions for optical fiber sensing technology in aircraft wing deformation measurement are summarized and put forward.</jats:p>

Smaller absolute values of G and ρ correspond to weaker thermal-optical effects. The maximum temperature deviation depends on laser power, contamination, bulk and coating absorption, and thermal conductivity; contamination can therefore increase heating and associated focus shift. Candidate athermal or low-effect materials identified in the excerpt include aThermoXX glass, calcium fluoride (CaF2), and crystalline quartz. The aThermoXX example shows no thermal focus shift despite thermal lensing, while crystalline quartz with its optic axis orthogonal to the optical axis is described as nearly exactly satisfying the self-compensation condition, producing neither thermal focus shift nor aberration even with contamination or surface absorption. Abstract:
Purpose
This paper aims to investigate the influence of non-uniform gas speed across the build area on the melt pool depth during laser powder bed fusion. The study focuses on whether a non-uniform gas speed is a source of process variation within an individual build.


Design/methodology/approach
Parts with many single-track laser scans were printed and characterized in different locations across the build area coupled with corresponding gas speed profile measurements. Cross-sectional melt pool depth, width, and area are compared against build location/gas speed profiles, scan direction, and laser scan speed.


Findings
The study shows that the melt pool depth of single-track laser scans produced on parts are highly variable. Despite this, trends were found showing a reduction in melt pool depth for slow laser scan speeds on the build platform near the inlet nozzle and when the laser scans are parallel to the gas flow direction.


Originality/value
A unique dataset of single-track laser scan cross-sectional melt pool measurements and gas speed measurements was generated to assess process variation associated with non-uniform gas speed. Additionally, a novel sample design was used to increase the number of single-track tests per part, which is widely applicable to studying process variation across the build area.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is of great importance for the visual measurement and analysis of the metallization process, which is the process of solid, liquid, and gas phase transformations of metal powders under high-energy laser irradiation due to the low boiling point/high saturated vapor pressure. Since the evaporation of metals involves the interaction of driving forces such as vapor back pressure, surface tension, and gravity, the movement of the melt pool is not stable. At the same time, it also produces vaporization products such as vapor plumes and sprays, which cause defects such as bubbles, porosity, lack of fusion, inclusions, etc., during the manufacturing process of the parts, affecting the performance and manufacturing quality of the parts. More and more researchers are using imaging technologies, such as high-speed X-ray, high-speed visible light cameras, and high-speed schlieren imaging, to perform noncontact visual measurements and analyses of the melt pool, vapor plume, and spatter during the metal evaporation process, and the results show that the metal evaporation process can be suppressed by optimizing the process parameters and changing the processing atmosphere, thereby reducing part defects and improving part performance and built part quality. This paper reviews the research on metal evaporation mechanisms and visual measurement methods of metal evaporation, then discusses the measures of metal evaporation, and finally summarizes and prospects the future research hotspots of LPBF technology, according to the existing scholars’ research on numerical simulation analysis and visual measurement methods of the metal evaporation process.

The excerpt directly addresses the severe reflection problem posed by highly reflective metals, although it does not specifically discuss LPBF or quantify the fraction of laser power returned into a fibre laser in an LPBF setup. It states that aluminium redirects approximately 92% of visible light and up to 98% of medium- and far-infrared radiation. Reflected laser light can travel back into the delivery fibres and cause damage. Copper is also difficult to process: at a 1 µm wavelength, it requires about six times the laser power needed to melt steel. The article notes that nickel-plating copper-based alloys can improve laser absorption and reduce the required power. The provided passage does not describe the resulting failure mechanisms in detail, nor does it explain protective measures such as optical isolators, beam tilting, angled processing, back-reflection monitoring, or internal laser/fibre protection. Consequently, those aspects would require additional sources. The wavelength dependence of absorptivity is emphasized, with solid-state/fibre lasers around 1 µm identified as relevant to processing reflective metals.

The excerpt states that copper reflects up to 95% of incident infrared laser energy around the approximately 1070 nm wavelength used in many LPBF systems; aluminum reflects approximately 90%. Because only a small fraction of the incident energy is initially absorbed, copper may fail to melt or sustain a stable melt pool. As copper approaches its melting point, absorptivity rises rapidly to 11–16%, producing process instability and increasing the tendency toward keyhole formation and spattering. The reflected energy can travel back through the optical system and damage laser components: the cited example reports damage to the optical coating on the laser mirror during copper LPBF. The supplied excerpt does not specify the reflected power in watts, nor does it discuss the requested protection strategies—optical isolators, beam or part tilting, or internal laser protection. It therefore supports percentage reflectivity and a documented damage mechanism, but not quantitative back-reflected power under particular laser settings or details of mitigation hardware. It also notes that powder has considerably higher absorptivity than bulk material because of increased surface area and multiple scattering, although this does not eliminate the risk associated with highly reflective copper.

It states that back-reflected light can potentially damage both the fibre-delivery optics and the laser itself. Several protection strategies are described. Optical isolators are used to control back-reflected light; for high-powered fibre lasers, the excerpt notes that isolators may require Faraday rotators and polarisers, which introduce power loss and possible beam degradation because of thermal effects. Another approach is to tilt or adjust the focus-head angle so reflected light is directed away from the laser. This reduces the risk of light coupling back into the laser, but compromises the beam spot: the spot becomes elliptical rather than circular, larger, and produces lower power density, slower processing, and greater heat input. Paul A. Hooper. Melt pool temperature and cooling rates in laser powder bed fusion. Additive Manufacturing, 22:548-559, Aug 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.addma.2018.05.032, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2018.05.032. This article has 1138 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes coaxial melt-pool monitoring integrated into a commercial Renishaw AM250 LPBF machine. A dichroic beamsplitter is installed in the laser path before the galvo scan head: laser-wavelength light continues through the scanner, while shorter-wavelength melt-pool radiation is reflected into a separate imaging enclosure. Relay lenses, a short-pass filter, a focusing lens, a second long-pass dichroic beamsplitter, and wavelength-specific band-pass filters route the emissions to two independently adjustable Photron FASTCAM SA5 high-speed cameras. The two-camera, two-wavelength arrangement supports thermographic temperature measurement while reducing sensitivity to unknown emissivity. A Thorlabs PDA10C photodiode is positioned on the reflected input side of the first dichroic beamsplitter to monitor input laser power. The coaxial arrangement keeps the melt pool centered during scanning and preserves spatial resolution across the build area. This excerpt does not identify dedicated instruments for beam profiling or scan-field calibration, nor does it describe pyrometers integrated directly into galvo scanner heads; it instead details camera-based two-wavelength thermography and photodiode power monitoring. It also notes that the commercial-machine modification preserves production-like gas flow, recoating, and other processing conditions.

## pqac-00000016

From text 'fox2024inprocessmonitoringand pages 44-47'.

Jason Fox, Felix Kim, Brandon Lane, Maxwell Praniewicz, Vipin Tondare, Jordan Weaver, and Paul Witherell. In-process monitoring and non-destructive evaluation for metal additive manufacturing processes. ArXiv, Sep 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.ir.8538, doi:10.6028/nist.ir.8538. This article has 16 citations.

The excerpt describes coaxial melt-pool monitoring (MPM) in LPBF as an optical arrangement in which photodetectors, pyrometers, or imaging sensors share the laser’s optical path. A dichroic mirror or beamsplitter is inserted into the laser path and selectively transmits and reflects different wavelengths. The approximately 1070 nm processing laser passes through the splitter and the galvanometer steering optics. Thermal/radiant emission from the melt pool travels back in the opposite direction, is separated from the laser by the beamsplitter, and is directed onto the coaxial detector. Additional beamsplitters can support multiple monitoring detectors. ## 1. Investigation of the thermal and optical performance of a spatial light modulator with high average power picosecond laser exposure for materials processing applications

Abstract:
Spatial light modulators (SLMs) addressed with computer generated holograms (CGHs) can create structured light fields on demand when an incident laser beam is diffracted by a phase CGH. The power handling limitations of these devices based on a liquid crystal layer has always been of some concern. With careful engineering of chip thermal management, we report the detailed optical phase and temperature response of a liquid cooled SLM exposed to picosecond laser powers up to 〈P〉  =  220 W at 1064 nm. This information is critical for determining device performance at high laser powers. SLM chip temperature rose linearly with incident laser exposure, increasing by only 5 °C at 〈P〉  =  220 W incident power, measured with a thermal imaging camera. Thermal response time with continuous exposure was 1–2 s. The optical phase response with incident power approaches 2π radians with average power up to 〈P〉  =  130 W, hence the operational limit, while above this power, liquid crystal thickness variations limit phase response to just over πradians. Modelling of the thermal and phase response with exposure is also presented, supporting experimental observations well. These remarkable performance characteristics show that liquid crystal based SLM technology is highly robust when efficiently cooled. High speed, multi-beam plasmonic surface micro-structuring at a rate R  =  8 cm2 s−1 is achieved on polished metal surfaces at 〈P〉  =  25 W exposure while diffractive, multi-beam surface ablation with average power 〈P〉  =100 W on stainless steel is demonstrated with ablation rate of ~4 mm3 min−1. However, above 130 W, first order diffraction efficiency drops significantly in accord with the observed operational limit. Continuous exposure for a period of 45 min at a laser power of 〈P〉  =  160 W did not result in any detectable drop in diffraction efficiency, confirmed afterwards by the efficient parallel beam processing at 〈P〉  =  100 W. Hence, no permanent changes in SLM phase response characteristics have been detected. This research work will help to accelerate the use of liquid crystal spatial light modulators for both scientific and ultra high throughput laser-materials micro-structuring applications.

## pqac-00000027

From text 'grantham2016opticaldesignand pages 2-4'.

Steven Grantham, Brandon Lane, Jorge Neira, Sergey Mekhontsev, Mihaela Vlasea, and Leonard Hanssen. Optical design and initial results from nist's ammt/temps facility. SPIE Proceedings, 9738:97380S, May 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1117/12.2214246, doi:10.1117/12.2214246. This article has 20 citations.

The excerpt describes NIST’s AMMT/TEMPS as an open, in-house LPBF platform designed to provide control and measurement access unavailable on commercial systems. A 500 W fiber laser is directed by a 3D optical scanner across a 100 mm × 100 mm build area. The shared optical train must support both high-power laser delivery and broadband measurement from approximately 400 nm to 10,000 nm; protected-silver mirrors are used, and an f-theta focusing lens is avoided so separate focusing/imaging optics can be used for the laser and TEMPS. The process-monitoring system uses a beamsplitter, filtered detectors, and a high-speed imager, with FPGA processing for real-time melt-pool monitoring and feedback control of scanner motion and laser power. The excerpt does not identify a dedicated commercial beam profiler or standalone power meter by name; the high-speed imager/detector suite is the stated monitoring instrumentation. TEMPS includes filtered radiometers, an FT spectrometer, an array spectrometer, a retractable hemispherical reflectometer, calibration sources, and reflectance standards. These tools support commissioning through optical alignment, laser/process monitoring, temperature measurement, reflectance/emissivity calibration, and verification of scanner and beam-path performance.

The excerpt describes NIST’s AMMT/TEMPS as an open-architecture laser powder-bed-fusion platform intended to provide machine-independent monitoring and control. Its optical system includes in-line visible-light collection optics, with multiple sensors arranged coaxially with the processing laser and/or positioned to observe the build bed from a stationary location. The testbed permits control of laser spot size, optical power, scan speed, hatch parameters, and other build variables. AMMT monitoring uses coaxial detectors and an imager to observe melt-pool behavior; sensor signals are processed in real time using an FPGA and can support feedback control of laser power and scan velocity. The excerpt also identifies optical measurement objectives, including high-speed imaging and photodetection, and describes TEMPS equipment such as a retractable reflectometer, calibration sources, and reflectance standards inside the process chamber. However, these pages do not specify the particular beam profiler, power meter, or detailed commissioning instrument set used for the LPBF optical system. They establish the system’s functional architecture and calibration concept but not the requested instrument models or complete commissioning procedure.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'abeyta2024anexperimentalapproach pages 21-26'.

A Abeyta. An experimental approach for characterizing gas flow in the build chamber of laser powder bed fusion systems utilizing particle image velocimetry. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt gives one representative gas-cross-flow condition for a commercial LPBF machine: Reijonen et al. evaluated an SLM 125 with an inlet flow of 4 m/s. However, it does not establish a universal cross-flow velocity used across commercial LPBF machines. It also does not specify the flow rate required to protect the optical window from spatter and metal vapor condensate. The cited discussion indicates that inert-gas cross-flow is important for managing the vapor plume and reducing laser-beam attenuation; without flow, the plume becomes enlarged and chaotic. Regarding part quality, the excerpt reports that regions with lower gas-flow speeds corresponded to higher porosity. Thus, weaker or nonuniform flow is associated with increased porosity, while effective flow helps reduce plume-related laser attenuation and defect formation. No direct relationship between cross-flow velocity and melt-pool depth is provided in this passage. The text discusses melt-pool monitoring generally, but does not report measurements showing how changing gas velocity changes melt-pool depth. Therefore, the excerpt supports a 4 m/s inlet example and a qualitative relationship between lower flow and higher porosity, but lacks the requested optical-window protection flow rate and quantitative melt-pool-depth dependence.

The excerpt does not provide a universal gas cross-flow velocity used in commercial LPBF machines, nor does it specify a volumetric flow rate required specifically to protect an optical window from spatter or condensate. It reports experiments using nominal velocities including 1, 2, and 4 m/s, and suggests that approximately 2 m/s was the minimum shielding-gas velocity needed for quality parts in the particular LPBF system studied. Below 2 m/s, spatter and vapor rise more vertically and are less effectively swept away. This reduced cross-flow is associated with a sharp reduction in melt-pool penetration, attributed partly to laser attenuation by the vapor plume; at 2 m/s and below, the process can shift from keyhole/transition melting toward conduction-mode melting. Reduced gas flow generally increases porosity. At high flow, effective plume removal and maintenance of a deep keyhole can produce gas or keyhole porosity, especially at high energy density and low scanning speeds. When flow is reduced enough to eliminate the deep keyhole, keyhole porosity decreases or disappears, although lack-of-fusion porosity can begin appearing at about 1 m/s. Local velocity and flow distribution across the build platform are machine-specific, so the reported velocities cannot be directly generalized to all commercial systems.

resulting in a relatively low absolute TOR value, fluorite is rarely used in industrial optics
because of some drawbacks in optical machining: the softness of the material prevents high-
