The excerpt describes NIST’s AMMT/TEMPS as an open-architecture laser powder-bed-fusion platform intended to provide machine-independent monitoring and control. Its optical system includes in-line visible-light collection optics, with multiple sensors arranged coaxially with the processing laser and/or positioned to observe the build bed from a stationary location. The testbed permits control of laser spot size, optical power, scan speed, hatch parameters, and other build variables. AMMT monitoring uses coaxial detectors and an imager to observe melt-pool behavior; sensor signals are processed in real time using an FPGA and can support feedback control of laser power and scan velocity. The excerpt also identifies optical measurement objectives, including high-speed imaging and photodetection, and describes TEMPS equipment such as a retractable reflectometer, calibration sources, and reflectance standards inside the process chamber. However, these pages do not specify the particular beam profiler, power meter, or detailed commissioning instrument set used for the LPBF optical system. They establish the system’s functional architecture and calibration concept but not the requested instrument models or complete commissioning procedure.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'abeyta2024anexperimentalapproach pages 21-26'.

A Abeyta. An experimental approach for characterizing gas flow in the build chamber of laser powder bed fusion systems utilizing particle image velocimetry. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt gives one representative gas-cross-flow condition for a commercial LPBF machine: Reijonen et al. evaluated an SLM 125 with an inlet flow of 4 m/s. However, it does not establish a universal cross-flow velocity used across commercial LPBF machines. It also does not specify the flow rate required to protect the optical window from spatter and metal vapor condensate. The cited discussion indicates that inert-gas cross-flow is important for managing the vapor plume and reducing laser-beam attenuation; without flow, the plume becomes enlarged and chaotic. Regarding part quality, the excerpt reports that regions with lower gas-flow speeds corresponded to higher porosity. Thus, weaker or nonuniform flow is associated with increased porosity, while effective flow helps reduce plume-related laser attenuation and defect formation. No direct relationship between cross-flow velocity and melt-pool depth is provided in this passage. The text discusses melt-pool monitoring generally, but does not report measurements showing how changing gas velocity changes melt-pool depth. Therefore, the excerpt supports a 4 m/s inlet example and a qualitative relationship between lower flow and higher porosity, but lacks the requested optical-window protection flow rate and quantitative melt-pool-depth dependence.

The excerpt does not provide a universal gas cross-flow velocity used in commercial LPBF machines, nor does it specify a volumetric flow rate required specifically to protect an optical window from spatter or condensate. It reports experiments using nominal velocities including 1, 2, and 4 m/s, and suggests that approximately 2 m/s was the minimum shielding-gas velocity needed for quality parts in the particular LPBF system studied. Below 2 m/s, spatter and vapor rise more vertically and are less effectively swept away. This reduced cross-flow is associated with a sharp reduction in melt-pool penetration, attributed partly to laser attenuation by the vapor plume; at 2 m/s and below, the process can shift from keyhole/transition melting toward conduction-mode melting. Reduced gas flow generally increases porosity. At high flow, effective plume removal and maintenance of a deep keyhole can produce gas or keyhole porosity, especially at high energy density and low scanning speeds. When flow is reduced enough to eliminate the deep keyhole, keyhole porosity decreases or disappears, although lack-of-fusion porosity can begin appearing at about 1 m/s. Local velocity and flow distribution across the build platform are machine-specific, so the reported velocities cannot be directly generalized to all commercial systems.

resulting in a relatively low absolute TOR value, fluorite is rarely used in industrial optics
because of some drawbacks in optical machining: the softness of the material prevents high-

   Undoped yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG, Y3Al5O12) is another optically isotropic crys-
tal which is well-known in laser techniques for its high thermal conductivity. Therefore, even
with a relatively high TCOP value, Fig. 8, and far location from the self-compensation blue solid
line, this crystal is characterized by a relatively low TOR value, similar to that of sapphire. This
makes undoped YAG an attractive material for optical windows and lenses operating with high-
power lasers; in addition, the hardness and good machining properties allow obtaining high-
quality optical surfaces. Important limitations of the use of undoped YAG in engineering practice
are the relatively high costs and available workpiece sizes, practically up to 1 inch. Nonetheless,
undoped YAG finds use in industrial optics, for example, as material for thermally loaded lenses
in zoom beam expanders for high-power linearly polarized lasers, when birefringent optical
materials, such as sapphire or crystalline quartz, cannot be applied.
   Polycrystalline ZnS is considered in some projects47,79 as an optical material for windows
and focusing optics owing to its high thermal conductivity, low absorption, and high refractive
index, Table 2, which allows making thin optical elements. However, other physical properties,
primarily high positive dn∕dT, lead to an extremely high TCOP value, Fig. 8, which does not
allow providing acceptable in engineering practice TOR, Fig. 9, even with high thermal con-
ductivity. As result, ZnS is not widely used in optics for high-power lasers with wavelengths
close to 1 μm.
   Crystalline quartz, obviously, demonstrates champion properties for high-power laser
optics owing to the matching of negative dn∕dT with CTE, high material purity, providing low
absorption of laser radiation, as well as relatively high thermal conductivity, ensuring effective
heat dissipation through optical surfaces. When the optic axis of a crystal is parallel to the
window optical surfaces or is orthogonal to the optical axis of the lens (SiO2-e), for example,
a waveplate, the self-compensation condition Eq. (59) is almost exactly fulfilled, and the SiO2-e
spot is located on the blue solid line in Fig. 8. Then, the absolute values of TCOP and TOR are
close to zero, which is of great importance for optics working with high-power lasers, since
ensures minimized thermo-optical effects even in the case of gradient heating because of either
cause, such as absorption of the laser energy in bulk material or in the anti-reflection coatings,
contamination, scratches and other defects on optical surfaces. When the optical elements are
implemented in such a way that the optic axis of a crystal is collinear to the optical axis of
the optical element (SiO2-o), there is a slight increase in the absolute values of TCOP and
TOR due to the anisotropy of dn∕dT, CTE and thermal conductivity. Nevertheless, even in this
case, the thermo-optical effects induced by the gradient heating are negligible and cause situa-
tions where experienced users of high-power lasers apply focusing optics made of crystalline
quartz with lasers of 10-kW power and 12-mm beam diameter and are surprised that there is
no thermal focus shift, even if the optics are contaminated during laser cutting. No doubts, the
thermo-optical characteristics TCOP and TOR, as well as good physical properties for optical
machining and coating, make crystalline quartz an excellent material for optics working with
multi-kW lasers. The birefringence of crystalline quartz should be taken into account as a poten-
tial cause of unwished effects in some specific cases of laser applications, for example, in the
case of modern linearly polarized high-power ultra-short pulse lasers. At the same time, the weak
birefringence of crystalline quartz does not limit the use of optical elements with multimode
multi-kW lasers, this point is considered in the next section.
   Sapphire is another well-suited crystalline optical material for high-power laser optics with
outstanding thermal conductivity ensuring efficient heat dissipation, low anisotropy in physical
properties such as dn∕dT, CTE and thermal conductivity. Other properties important for practice
are a broad transmission spectrum, high purity, and virtually no limitations on the size of optical
elements; the relatively high refractive index allows making thin optical elements and minimizes
the number of lenses in optical systems. Owing to high positive values of CTE and dn∕dT,

## pqac-00000042

From text 'ozgoren2011highpowerallfiber pages 65-70'.

K Özgören. High power all-fiber laser-amplifier systems for materials processing. Unknown journal, 2011.

The excerpt does not provide a burn-through time for a 500 W or 1 kW continuous-wave near-infrared laser, nor does it specify sheet thickness, alloy, beam diameter, focus, scan conditions, or cooling. It does identify the parameters needed to estimate penetration: wavelength-dependent reflectivity, thermal conductivity and diffusivity, evaporation temperature, and heat of evaporation. At approximately 1 μm, many metals including aluminum have reflectivity greater than 0.9, although reflectivity decreases as temperature rises. The excerpt contrasts steel as a poorer thermal conductor, which can develop higher local temperatures, with aluminum and copper as better conductors that spread heat more effectively. It also states that materials with lower evaporation temperature and heat of evaporation are easier to remove. Metallic absorption occurs within an approximately 10 nm optical penetration depth at 1 μm, with energy transferred from conduction electrons to the lattice. Consequently, the supplied text supports only a qualitative comparison: actual burn-through time cannot be determined from laser power alone and requires a transient heat-transfer/ablation calculation using the sheet and beam parameters.


---

## pqac-00000043

From text 'zuo2025highperformancenirlaserbeam pages 9-11'.

Shuchen Zuo, Shuai Wang, Cameron Pulham, Yin Tang, Walter Perrie, Olivier J. Allegre, Yue Tang, Martin Sharp, Jim Leach, David J. Whitehead, Matthew Bilton, Wajira Mirihanage, Paul Mativenga, Stuart P. Edwardson, and Geoff Dearden. High-performance nir laser-beam shaping and materials processing at 350 w with a spatial light modulator. Photonics, 12:544, May 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/photonics12060544, doi:10.3390/photonics12060544. This article has 11 citations.

The excerpt provides limited experimental information relevant to laser penetration of steel, but it does not report protective-housing burn-through times, single-beam penetration times, aluminium results, or tests at 500 W or 1 kW. In the described experiment, a 300 W near-infrared laser was used to create a five-spot pattern on polished mild steel with 5-second exposures. The reported total evaporation rate was approximately 0.7 mm³/min for the five-spot pattern, and individual spot evaporation-volume rates increased with power: 309 ± 70 µm³ W⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 100 W, 2221 ± 690 at 200 W, and 4429 ± 1208 at 300 W. The authors note substantial thermal diffusion during exposure, along with melting, plasma absorption, and nonuniformity, all of which affect material removal. Higher-power profiles widened, possibly because of thermal lensing. These measurements cannot be directly extrapolated to the time required for a 500 W or 1 kW CW beam to penetrate a steel or aluminium guard sheet, because penetration depends strongly on sheet thickness, alloy, reflectivity, beam diameter and intensity, focus, incidence angle, cooling, and whether the beam is stationary or scanned.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a summary table of the 7 beam delivery critique topics for the LPBF system, with columns: Topic, Key Risk/Issue, Quantitative Data, Mitigation/Recommendation. Cover: (1) Thermal focal shift, (2) F-theta lens suitability, (3) Back-reflection, (4) Window contamination, (5) Galvo aperture/spot ellipticity, (6) Commissioning instruments, (7) Laser safety. Use data from the evidence gathered: fused silica focal shift ~0.32 mm at 2.5 kW (contaminated), D*=0.55-1.27e-6 mm/W, aluminium reflectivity ~90% at 1 \u00b5m, gas cross-flow 2-4 m/s needed, etc."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Topic | Key Risk/Issue | Quantitative Data | Mitigation/Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Thermal focal shift | Absorption in fused silica, AR coatings, dirt and condensate creates radial temperature gradients, changing focus and adding aberration; contamination can dominate clean-bulk absorption. | A fingerprint-contaminated fused-silica lens shifted about −0.32 mm at 2.5 kW and −0.47 mm at 4.5 kW. Measured intensity-specific thermal refractive power was approximately 0.55 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for new, wavelength-specific-coated fused silica versus 1.16–1.27 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for used uncoated lenses. These results do not justify one universal 500 W shift because geometry and absorption matter. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002) | Establish cold and thermally soaked caustics with a focus monitor or Z-stack of low-duty-cycle marks; trend focus and transmitted power before every build and after window replacement. Keep optics clean and temperature stabilized. Consider crystalline quartz for highly loaded windows or lenses; its thermo-optical ratio can be about 0.0053 of fused silica in the favorable orientation. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041) |
| 2. F-theta lens suitability | A generic marking lens may have an adequate pulsed LIDT yet lack a guaranteed 500 W CW absorption, thermal-focus, polarization and contamination specification. CW suitability is governed chiefly by coating/bulk absorption and heat removal—not a nanosecond LIDT number. | High-quality wavelength-specific coatings produced roughly half the thermal refractive power measured for used uncoated fused-silica lenses; broadband coatings can add substantial thermal power. Fused-silica f-theta optics have nevertheless been used in LPBF with 500 W lasers and approximately 35 µm spots. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000038) | Do not qualify a low-cost lens from catalog LIDT alone. Require written approval for 500 W CW at 1070 nm, coating and total absorption data, clear aperture at every scan angle, thermal-focus data, and a warranty for the intended duty cycle. Prefer an industrial LPBF/welding-grade fused-silica assembly from a vendor that will thermally qualify the complete lens; verify it experimentally at staged power. |
| 3. Aluminium back-reflection | High total reflectance does not equal power recoupled into the fibre, but an occasional specular return aligned with the receive numerical aperture can destabilize or damage the delivery fibre, polymer components, coatings or laser source. | Aluminium reflects approximately 90% around 1070 nm; smooth surfaces can exceed 75%, whereas copper can approach 95–98%. The power returning to the source is normally only a fraction of output because the melt pool is rough, displaced from the waist and imperfectly normal to the beam; no defensible fixed wattage can be assigned without measurement. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014) | Obtain IPG’s written back-reflection limit and protection description for the exact serial-number configuration. Use source-side reflected-power monitoring and fast shutdown; add a properly rated free-space isolator only if IPG and the scanner integrator approve its thermal load. Avoid the exact field center for stationary exposures, prohibit firing on smooth bare plate at normal incidence, and use a small intentional optical/window wedge or tilt whose returned ray is traced into a beam dump—not merely displaced onto another optic. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013) |
| 4. Window and cover-slide contamination | Mg/Zn-rich condensate and spatter absorb and scatter the beam, reduce delivered power and create local hot spots that can crack the sacrificial slide or damage its coating. Published deposition-rate and replacement-interval data are sparse and strongly machine/alloy dependent. | In one LPBF study, reducing nominal cross-flow from 4 to 2 m/s reduced melt-pool cross-sectional area by 30–50%; 2.5–4.0 m/s cleared plume and bent spatter downstream, while porosity rose rapidly at ≤2.0 m/s. A modified two-row nozzle increased overall spatter removal from 69% to 93%. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000021) | The proposed 2.5–3 m/s is plausible only if measured uniformly over the complete bed. Add a separate clean-argon gas knife immediately below the sacrificial slide and a broad, laminar bed cross-flow into a close-coupled exhaust. A porous flow straightener can suppress turbulence; a top inlet flowing away from the window prevents rising condensate from reaching it. Inspect and measure transmission before each build; replace by a power-loss/hot-spot criterion rather than an assumed hour interval. (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045) |
| 5. Galvo aperture and edge spot | A nominal 20 mm entrance aperture does not guarantee adequate clear aperture on both moving mirrors at all scan angles. Clipping of a Gaussian tail heats an edge and produces asymmetric diffraction; off-axis incidence also elongates the work-plane spot. | For a 75 mm-diameter field, the paraxial chief-ray angles are arctan(37.5/160) ≈ 13.2° for f = 160 mm and arctan(37.5/254) ≈ 8.4° for f = 254 mm. Simple projection gives a tangential geometric stretch of only 1/cosθ ≈ 1.027 and 1.011, respectively, but scanner/lens aberrations can be larger. Edge elongation is associated with lower melt-pool depth in some scan orientations and increased roughness or lack-of-fusion. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) | Treat 7.5 mm as the safer starting beam for a 20 mm basiCube; 5 mm increases the diffraction-limited waist by about 50%. Require the scanner/lens vendor’s footprint and clear-aperture trace; as a conservative alignment target, keep the worst-case clear semi-aperture ≥1.5 times the Gaussian 1/e² radius. Measure caustic, power, ellipticity and centroid at center, axes and corners after thermal soak. |
| 6. Commissioning and monitoring | Nominal laser power, catalog spot size and visible pilot alignment do not establish delivered power, focus, M², field geometry or thermal stability. | NIST’s open LPBF testbed uses a 500 W fibre laser and beamsplitter-based coaxial monitoring. LPBF beam-characterization tools reported in the literature include Focus Beam Profiler, BeamWatch AM, FocusMonitor+ and 3-D Beam Mapper. Coaxial monitoring passes the approximately 1070 nm process beam through a dichroic while routing returning melt-pool emission to photodiodes or cameras. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) | Minimum kit: calibrated ≥600 W thermopile or water-cooled calorimeter; sampling optic and dump; beam profiler/focus monitor capable of approximately 75 µm caustics; low-power 1070 nm card/viewer; removable visible alignment source; microscope; thermal camera for optics; and engraved/anodized calibration plates plus a metrology microscope for affine and higher-order field correction. For monitoring, a fast coaxial Si or InGaAs photodiode is the simplest fit; add an off-axis global camera first, then two-band pyrometry if calibrated temperature—not merely intensity—is required. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) |
| 7. {"answer": "# Critique of the Beam Delivery System for a Lab-Built 500 W Aluminium LPBF Machine

## Overview

The proposed optical train—IPG YLR-500-SM → QBH collimator → SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo → fused-silica f-theta lens (f = 160 or 254 mm) → AR-coated fused-silica chamber window → sacrificial cover slide → argon atmosphere—is architecturally conventional for a small LPBF platform. However, aluminium alloys with volatile elements (Mg, Zn) and high reflectivity introduce specific beam-delivery hazards that require careful engineering beyond catalogue component selection. The following critique addresses each of the seven topics with quantitative data where available.

The summary table below consolidates the key findings for each topic area:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## 1. Thermal Focal Shift of Fused-Silica Optics

Fused silica has a high temperature coefficient of optical path length (TCOP, G ≈ 9.03 × 10⁻⁶/K), and its relatively low thermal conductivity (≈1.31 W/m·K) produces steep radial temperature gradients under absorbed laser power, resulting in strong negative focal shift (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000001). Experimentally, a contaminated (fingerprint) fused-silica focusing lens showed a focal shift of −0.32 mm at 2.5 kW and −0.47 mm at 4.5 kW, in reasonable agreement with calculated values of −0.31 and −0.40 mm respectively (pqac-00000000). At 500 W, the absolute shift scales approximately linearly with absorbed power, but the absorbed fraction depends critically on coating quality and surface cleanliness. Faas et al. measured an intensity-specific thermal refractive power D* of 0.55 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for a new fused-silica lens with a high-quality wavelength-specific coating, versus 1.16–1.27 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for used, uncoated fused-silica lenses (pqac-00000002). Broadband coatings introduce substantially greater thermal power than the substrate alone (pqac-00000006).

**Contamination effect.** Even a fingerprint or thin dust layer on a fused-silica window in a welding shop or SLM chamber creates a temperature gradient that shifts the focus and distorts the spot profile (pqac-00000039). This is especially relevant for aluminium LPBF where Mg and Zn condensate continuously deposits on optics.

**Athermal alternatives.** Crystalline quartz (SiO₂, extraordinary orientation) has near-zero TCOP and thermo-optical ratio (TOR ≈ −0.04 × 10⁻⁶ W/m vs. 6.89 × 10⁻⁶ W/m for fused silica), fulfilling the self-compensation condition almost exactly. Sapphire achieves a low TOR (0.38–0.39 × 10⁻⁶ W/m) through extremely high thermal conductivity despite a high TCOP. The specialty glass aThermoXX (TCOP ≈ −0.31 × 10⁻⁶/K) offers near-zero thermal lensing and is used for SLM protective windows at power densities up to about 3 kW/cm² (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041). Undoped YAG is another candidate for high-power windows, with good hardness and machining properties, though available sizes are typically limited to about 1 inch (pqac-00000041).

**Detection and compensation.** LPBF builders should perform Z-scan burn tests (a staircase of single tracks at varying Z-offset) at cold start and after thermal soak to quantify the focal shift in situ. Trending delivered power and focal position before every build using an inline or removable focus monitor is essential. The relationship Δf/z_R ≈ −D* × P/(λ × M²) can be used for first-order estimation (pqac-00000007).

---

## 2. F-Theta Lens Suitability at 500 W CW

A catalogue marking-grade f-theta lens (Thorlabs FTH series or similar) is typically specified with a pulsed laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT), which is not directly applicable to CW operation. At 500 W CW, the governing failure mode is not instantaneous optical damage but cumulative thermal degradation: coating absorption, thermal lensing, and thermally induced stress. The coating is the dominant thermal contributor—broadband coatings can produce roughly double the thermal refractive power of an uncoated substrate (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006).

Fused-silica f-theta lenses have been successfully used in LPBF at 500 W with a 35 µm spot for copper processing, though this required careful attention to thermal effects (pqac-00000038). Commercial LPBF machines (EOS, SLM Solutions, Renishaw) typically use industrial-grade fused-silica f-theta lenses from suppliers such as Sill Optics or Linos/Excelitas, which are specifically rated and warranty-qualified for CW multi-hundred-watt operation. These are generally non-telecentric designs for smaller machines, with telecentric lenses reserved for larger scan fields where constant spot size and normal incidence are critical.

**Recommendation.** Do not qualify a low-cost lens from its pulsed LIDT number alone. Require from the vendor: (a) total absorption specification at 1070 nm CW, (b) thermal focal shift data at the intended power and duty cycle, (c) clear aperture trace at all scan angles for the intended beam diameter, and (d) a warranty covering the CW operating conditions. If the vendor cannot provide this data, budget for an industrial LPBF-grade lens (Sill S4LFT or comparable).

---

## 3. Back-Reflection from Aluminium Melt Pools

Aluminium reflects approximately 90% of 1070 nm radiation from a polished bulk surface; copper can exceed 95% (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). However, the fraction actually recoupled into the delivery fibre in LPBF is much smaller because: the melt pool is rough and displaced from the beam waist; the surface is not normal to the beam at most scan positions; and the collection solid angle of the return path through the f-theta and galvo is limited (pqac-00000011). Nevertheless, even a brief specular return during initial melting on a smooth build plate can deliver dangerous power spikes.

**Damage mechanisms.** Back-reflected light travelling through the delivery optics can overheat polymer fibre components, damage optical coatings on the galvo mirrors, and destabilise or damage the laser source (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000009). Copper LPBF studies have documented optical mirror coating damage during high-power processing (pqac-00000038).

**Protection strategies.** Several approaches are used in practice:

- **Laser internal protection:** Modern IPG YLR-series lasers include an internal back-reflection monitor and automatic power shutdown when reflected power exceeds a threshold. The YLR-500-SM likely tolerates some reflected power, but the exact specification should be obtained from IPG for the specific serial number configuration (pqac-00000013).
- **Free-space isolators:** Faraday isolators provide high isolation (>30 dB) but introduce insertion loss, thermal load, and potential beam degradation; at 500 W single-mode they are expensive and require careful thermal management (pqac-00000010).
- **Beam dump and monitoring:** JK Lasers/IPG developed systems that redirect back-reflected light into a beam dump and continuously monitor reflection levels, automatically shutting down the laser when limits are exceeded (pqac-00000013).
- **Tilting the processing head/window:** Tilting diverts specular returns away from the fibre but produces an elliptical, larger spot with lower power density and potentially increased heat input (pqac-00000010).
- **Operational protocols:** Avoid stationary exposure at the exact field centre, never fire at full power on a bare polished build plate, use a roughened or pre-coated plate surface, and begin scanning immediately upon laser turn-on (pqac-00000014).

---

## 4. Window and Cover-Slide Contamination

**Contamination sources.** Aluminium alloys containing Mg and Zn produce significant metal vapour during LPBF. This vapour condenses as fine nanoparticulate (condensate) that, together with ejected melt-pool spatter, deposits on the chamber window and sacrificial cover slide. The condensate attenuates the laser beam through both absorption and scattering, and creates local hot spots that can nucleate thermal damage on the optics (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000022).

**Effect on delivered power.** Reducing shielding gas cross-flow from 4 m/s to 2 m/s in one study decreased melt-pool cross-sectional area by 30–50%, primarily attributed to laser attenuation by the uncleared vapour plume (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000031). Most vaporised condensate particles concentrate below approximately 1 mm above the keyhole, so attenuation is strongest near the interaction zone (pqac-00000024).

**Gas flow requirements.** A cross-flow velocity of approximately 2.5–4.0 m/s above the powder bed effectively clears the vapour plume and bends spatter trajectories downstream (pqac-00000032). Below 2.0 m/s, porosity increases exponentially and process stability degrades (pqac-00000031). A modified two-row nozzle arrangement increased spatter removal efficiency from 69% to 93% (pqac-00000021). The proposed 2.5–3 m/s cross-flow is at the lower end of the effective range.

**Window protection design.** Patents for LPBF machines describe a dual gas-inlet architecture: a horizontal cross-flow across the bed for plume/spatter removal, plus a separate downward-flowing "gas knife" adjacent to the transmission element (window) that creates a curtain of clean gas preventing rising condensate from reaching the optics (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000044). Porous sintered-metal or fibre-web flow straighteners with 20–90% porosity and 1–10 mm pore sizes produce laminar flow and uniform velocity profiles (pqac-00000044). Commercial practice is to clean the optical window after every build (pqac-00000020).

**Window tilting.** A slight wedge or tilt on the chamber window (1–2°) prevents ghost reflections from the window surfaces from propagating back along the beam path into the galvo and fibre. This is standard practice on many LPBF machines and highly recommended.

**Recommendation for volatile alloys.** For Mg/Zn-bearing aluminium alloys, budget for sacrificial cover slides changed every 1–3 builds (more frequent for high-Mg alloys), supplement the bed cross-flow with a dedicated window gas knife, and monitor transmitted power with a photodiode on the return path of a dichroic beamsplitter.

---

## 5. Galvo Aperture Clipping, Mirror Heating, and Edge Effects

**Beam-to-aperture margin.** The SCANLAB basiCube 20 has a 20 mm entrance aperture. With a 7.5 mm collimated beam (1/e² diameter), the beam-to-aperture ratio is 20/7.5 ≈ 2.67, which provides adequate margin against clipping on the entry mirror. With a 5 mm beam, this ratio increases to 4.0, which is safer for clipping but produces a larger diffraction-limited spot (scaling inversely with beam diameter on the lens). As a conservative design rule, the worst-case clear semi-aperture at any scan angle should be ≥1.5× the 1/e² beam radius.

**Mirror heating.** The basiCube mirrors are rated for approximately 1 kW at 1064 nm without active cooling. At 500 W CW with high-quality dielectric coatings (absorption <0.1%), thermal loading on each mirror is approximately 0.5 W, which is manageable without cooling for typical scan patterns. However, long dwell times on a single mirror position (e.g., during hatch scanning near one field edge) increase local heating and may introduce transient pointing drift.

**Angle of incidence and spot ellipticity.** For a 75 mm diameter scan field with f = 160 mm, the maximum half-field scan angle is arctan(37.5/160) ≈ 13.2°. With f = 254 mm, this reduces to arctan(37.5/254) ≈ 8.4°. The geometric spot elongation from oblique incidence on the powder bed is 1/cos θ, giving 1.027× at 13.2° and 1.011× at 8.4°—modest in themselves. However, combined scanner and lens aberrations produce measurable spot elongation at field edges (pqac-00000025). The beam is approximately circular only at the build-plane centre and becomes increasingly elliptical with radial distance (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). This elongation causes position-dependent changes in effective power density and melt-pool depth: perpendicular elongation reduces penetration, while parallel elongation can partially compensate through increased interaction time (pqac-00000026). Edge-of-field positions show increased porosity and surface roughness (pqac-00000025).

**Recommendation.** Use f = 254 mm for a 75 mm field (8.4° max angle) rather than f = 160 mm (13.2°), accepting a larger nominal spot. Measure caustic, power, ellipticity, and centroid at centre, mid-axes, and corners after thermal stabilisation to build a field-correction map.

---

## 6. Commissioning Instruments and Melt-Pool Monitoring

**Beam characterisation.** NIST's open-architecture AMMT/TEMPS LPBF platform uses a 500 W fibre laser with a shared optical train supporting both high-power delivery and broadband measurement, including filtered detectors and a high-speed imager with FPGA-based real-time processing (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). Commercial LPBF beam-characterisation tools reported in the literature include the Focus Beam Profiler (FBP), BeamWatch AM (BWAM), FocusMonitor+ (FM+), and 3-D Beam Mapper; the latter is used to map beam characteristics across the entire working envelope (pqac-00000029).

**Minimum commissioning kit:**
- **Power meter:** Calibrated thermopile or water-cooled calorimeter rated ≥600 W (e.g., Ophir 500A-BB-34 or Coherent LM-500).
- **Beam profiler / focus finder:** A system capable of measuring ≈75 µm caustics (e.g., Primes FocusMonitor, Ophir BeamWatch, or Spiricon pyroelectric array with appropriate attenuation).
- **IR viewer / detector card:** 1070 nm sensitive cards or phosphor-coated viewers for alignment.
- **Visible alignment laser:** A co-aligned HeNe or red diode for coarse optical path verification.
- **Scan-field calibration:** Engraved or anodised stainless-steel calibration plates marked at known grid positions, plus a metrology microscope or optical CMM for affine and higher-order field correction.
- **Thermal camera:** For monitoring optic temperatures during power ramp.

**Melt-pool monitoring.** Coaxial monitoring in LPBF uses a dichroic beamsplitter inserted into the laser path before the galvo scanner head: the ≈1070 nm processing beam passes through, while shorter-wavelength thermal radiation from the melt pool is reflected to sensors (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). Commercial implementations include the Renishaw AM250's dual-camera system using two Photron FASTCAM SA5 high-speed cameras with wavelength-specific bandpass filters for two-colour thermography, plus a Thorlabs PDA10C photodiode for laser power monitoring (pqac-00000015). Two-wavelength pyrometers using InGaAs photodiodes enable emissivity-independent temperature estimation (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000017).

For a basiCube-class head, the simplest fit is a fast coaxial Si or InGaAs photodiode (sensitive to thermal emission in the 900–1700 nm range) fed via a dichroic beamsplitter and laser-line notch filter, providing a scalar melt-pool intensity signal correlated with temperature and pool size. An off-axis global-view camera (visible or SWIR) adds layer-by-layer imaging capability. Full two-band coaxial pyrometry requires calibrated optics and careful field-of-view registration.

---

## 7. Laser Safety Optics

**Viewing windows for a Class 1 enclosure.** For a 1070 nm fibre laser at 500 W, viewing windows in the enclosure must attenuate any conceivable direct or scattered beam to below the Class 1 accessible emission limit (AEL). An optical density of OD 7 at 1070 nm attenuates 500 W to 50 nW, which is well below the CW Class 1 AEL at this wavelength (pqac-00000014). The required OD must be calculated per IEC 60825-1 from the specific viewing geometry, wavelength band, and exposure duration. Certified laser-safety filter glass (e.g., Laservision, Kentek, or NOIR) rated for the 1000–1100 nm band with OD ≥7 is recommended. Polycarbonate with appropriate absorptive filter dyes is another option, but glass filter windows are more resistant to surface damage and degradation.

**Guard and enclosure burn-through.** IEC 60825-4 (and ANSI Z136.1) require that protective housings withstand the maximum foreseeable laser exposure for a specified guard time. Burn-through time for 1.6 mm aluminium sheet exposed to a 500 W CW beam at 1070 nm is not a fixed number—it depends strongly on spot size (focused vs. defocused), beam intensity profile, alloy thermal conductivity, surface reflectivity, and cooling (pqac-00000042). Aluminium's high reflectivity at 1 µm (>90%) initially reflects most incident power, dramatically slowing penetration compared to steel; once absorption increases at elevated temperature, thermal conductivity rapidly conducts heat away from the spot (pqac-00000042). For a defocused beam (as would typically strike a guard panel), the irradiance may be well below the absorption-coupled melting threshold, potentially preventing penetration entirely.

**Practical guidance:** Prefer steel guards (1.5–3 mm mild steel) over aluminium for the beam enclosure, as steel has lower reflectivity and conductivity at 1 µm, providing more predictable guard behaviour. Use double-walled construction with an air gap. Install beam traps at foreseeable direct-beam impingement points. Interlock all doors, removable panels, window shutters, and monitor loss of coolant/flow and scanner faults. Commission the entire enclosure through a formal laser safety assessment per IEC 60825-1/IEC 60825-4, including a hazard analysis and, ideally, an empirical guard penetration test at maximum power with the worst-case focused beam geometry. Do not rely solely on a calculated burn-through time (pqac-00000042).

---

## Summary of Key Concerns

The proposed beam path is feasible but demands attention to several aluminium-specific risks: (1) thermal focal shift in fused-silica optics can exceed the Rayleigh range even at 500 W if surfaces become contaminated with Mg/Zn condensate—crystalline quartz or aThermoXX alternatives should be considered at minimum for the chamber window (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041); (2) catalogue marking-grade f-theta lenses lack CW thermal qualification; (3) back-reflection from aluminium mandates verified laser protection and operational protocols (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013); (4) volatile-element condensate requires a dedicated window gas knife in addition to the bed cross-flow (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045); (5) a 7.5 mm beam with f = 254 mm is preferred over f = 160 mm for edge-spot quality over a 75 mm field (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026); (6) a minimum set of beam-characterisation and monitoring tools must be budgeted from the outset (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029); and (7) laser-safety design should use steel guards, OD ≥7 viewing filters, and a formal IEC 60825 hazard analysis rather than relying on aluminium burn-through estimates."}

## Overview

The proposed optical train—IPG YLR-500-SM → QBH collimator → SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo → fused-silica f-theta lens (f = 160 or 254 mm) → AR-coated fused-silica chamber window → sacrificial cover slide → argon atmosphere—is architecturally conventional for a small LPBF platform. However, aluminium alloys with volatile elements (Mg, Zn) and high reflectivity introduce specific beam-delivery hazards that require careful engineering beyond catalogue component selection. The following critique addresses each of the seven topics with quantitative data where available.

The summary table below consolidates the key findings for each topic area:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## 1. Thermal Focal Shift of Fused-Silica Optics

Fused silica has a high temperature coefficient of optical path length (TCOP, G ≈ 9.03 × 10⁻⁶/K), and its relatively low thermal conductivity (≈1.31 W/m·K) produces steep radial temperature gradients under absorbed laser power, resulting in strong negative focal shift (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000001). Experimentally, a contaminated (fingerprint) fused-silica focusing lens showed a focal shift of −0.32 mm at 2.5 kW and −0.47 mm at 4.5 kW, in reasonable agreement with calculated values of −0.31 and −0.40 mm respectively (pqac-00000000). At 500 W, the absolute shift scales approximately linearly with absorbed power, but the absorbed fraction depends critically on coating quality and surface cleanliness. Faas et al. measured an intensity-specific thermal refractive power D* of 0.55 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for a new fused-silica lens with a high-quality wavelength-specific coating, versus 1.16–1.27 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for used, uncoated fused-silica lenses (pqac-00000002). Broadband coatings introduce substantially greater thermal power than the substrate alone (pqac-00000006).

**Contamination effect.** Even a fingerprint or thin dust layer on a fused-silica window in a welding shop or SLM chamber creates a temperature gradient that shifts the focus and distorts the spot profile (pqac-00000039). This is especially relevant for aluminium LPBF where Mg and Zn condensate continuously deposits on optics.

**Athermal alternatives.** Crystalline quartz (SiO₂, extraordinary orientation) has near-zero TCOP and thermo-optical ratio (TOR ≈ −0.04 × 10⁻⁶ W/m vs. 6.89 × 10⁻⁶ W/m for fused silica), fulfilling the self-compensation condition almost exactly. Sapphire achieves a low TOR (0.38–0.39 × 10⁻⁶ W/m) through extremely high thermal conductivity despite a high TCOP. The specialty glass aThermoXX (TCOP ≈ −0.31 × 10⁻⁶/K) offers near-zero thermal lensing and is used for SLM protective windows at power densities up to about 3 kW/cm² (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041). Undoped YAG is another candidate for high-power windows, with good hardness and machining properties, though available sizes are typically limited to about 1 inch (pqac-00000041).

**Detection and compensation.** LPBF builders should perform Z-scan burn tests (a staircase of single tracks at varying Z-offset) at cold start and after thermal soak to quantify the focal shift in situ. Trending delivered power and focal position before every build using an inline or removable focus monitor is essential. The relationship Δf/z_R ≈ −D* × P/(λ × M²) can be used for first-order estimation (pqac-00000007).

---

## 2. F-Theta Lens Suitability at 500 W CW

A catalogue marking-grade f-theta lens (Thorlabs FTH series or similar) is typically specified with a pulsed laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT), which is not directly applicable to CW operation. At 500 W CW, the governing failure mode is not instantaneous optical damage but cumulative thermal degradation: coating absorption, thermal lensing, and thermally induced stress. The coating is the dominant thermal contributor—broadband coatings can produce roughly double the thermal refractive power of an uncoated substrate (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006).

Fused-silica f-theta lenses have been successfully used in LPBF at 500 W with a 35 µm spot for copper processing, though this required careful attention to thermal effects (pqac-00000038). Commercial LPBF machines (EOS, SLM Solutions, Renishaw) typically use industrial-grade fused-silica f-theta lenses from suppliers such as Sill Optics or Linos/Excelitas, which are specifically rated and warranty-qualified for CW multi-hundred-watt operation. These are generally non-telecentric designs for smaller machines, with telecentric lenses reserved for larger scan fields where constant spot size and normal incidence are critical.

**Recommendation.** Do not qualify a low-cost lens from its pulsed LIDT number alone. Require from the vendor: (a) total absorption specification at 1070 nm CW, (b) thermal focal shift data at the intended power and duty cycle, (c) clear aperture trace at all scan angles for the intended beam diameter, and (d) a warranty covering the CW operating conditions. If the vendor cannot provide this data, budget for an industrial LPBF-grade lens (Sill S4LFT or comparable).

---

## 3. Back-Reflection from Aluminium Melt Pools

Aluminium reflects approximately 90% of 1070 nm radiation from a polished bulk surface; copper can exceed 95% (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). However, the fraction actually recoupled into the delivery fibre in LPBF is much smaller because: the melt pool is rough and displaced from the beam waist; the surface is not normal to the beam at most scan positions; and the collection solid angle of the return path through the f-theta and galvo is limited (pqac-00000011). Nevertheless, even a brief specular return during initial melting on a smooth build plate can deliver dangerous power spikes.

**Damage mechanisms.** Back-reflected light travelling through the delivery optics can overheat polymer fibre components, damage optical coatings on the galvo mirrors, and destabilise or damage the laser source (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000009). Copper LPBF studies have documented optical mirror coating damage during high-power processing (pqac-00000038).

**Protection strategies.** Several approaches are used in practice:

- **Laser internal protection:** Modern IPG YLR-series lasers include an internal back-reflection monitor and automatic power shutdown when reflected power exceeds a threshold. The YLR-500-SM likely tolerates some reflected power, but the exact specification should be obtained from IPG for the specific serial number configuration (pqac-00000013).
- **Free-space isolators:** Faraday isolators provide high isolation (>30 dB) but introduce insertion loss, thermal load, and potential beam degradation; at 500 W single-mode they are expensive and require careful thermal management (pqac-00000010).
- **Beam dump and monitoring:** JK Lasers/IPG developed systems that redirect back-reflected light into a beam dump and continuously monitor reflection levels, automatically shutting down the laser when limits are exceeded (pqac-00000013).
- **Tilting the processing head/window:** Tilting diverts specular returns away from the fibre but produces an elliptical, larger spot with lower power density and potentially increased heat input (pqac-00000010).
- **Operational protocols:** Avoid stationary exposure at the exact field centre, never fire at full power on a bare polished build plate, use a roughened or pre-coated plate surface, and begin scanning immediately upon laser turn-on (pqac-00000014).

---

## 4. Window and Cover-Slide Contamination

**Contamination sources.** Aluminium alloys containing Mg and Zn produce significant metal vapour during LPBF. This vapour condenses as fine nanoparticulate (condensate) that, together with ejected melt-pool spatter, deposits on the chamber window and sacrificial cover slide. The condensate attenuates the laser beam through both absorption and scattering, and creates local hot spots that can nucleate thermal damage on the optics (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000022).

**Effect on delivered power.** Reducing shielding gas cross-flow from 4 m/s to 2 m/s in one study decreased melt-pool cross-sectional area by 30–50%, primarily attributed to laser attenuation by the uncleared vapour plume (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000031). Most vaporised condensate particles concentrate below approximately 1 mm above the keyhole, so attenuation is strongest near the interaction zone (pqac-00000024).

**Gas flow requirements.** A cross-flow velocity of approximately 2.5–4.0 m/s above the powder bed effectively clears the vapour plume and bends spatter trajectories downstream (pqac-00000032). Below 2.0 m/s, porosity increases exponentially and process stability degrades (pqac-00000031). A modified two-row nozzle arrangement increased spatter removal efficiency from 69% to 93% (pqac-00000021). The proposed 2.5–3 m/s cross-flow is at the lower end of the effective range.

**Window protection design.** Patents for LPBF machines describe a dual gas-inlet architecture: a horizontal cross-flow across the bed for plume/spatter removal, plus a separate downward-flowing "gas knife" adjacent to the transmission element (window) that creates a curtain of clean gas preventing rising condensate from reaching the optics (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000044). Porous sintered-metal or fibre-web flow straighteners with 20–90% porosity and 1–10 mm pore sizes produce laminar flow and uniform velocity profiles (pqac-00000044). Commercial practice is to clean the optical window after every build (pqac-00000020).

**Window tilting.** A slight wedge or tilt on the chamber window (1–2°) prevents ghost reflections from the window surfaces from propagating back along the beam path into the galvo and fibre. This is standard practice on many LPBF machines and highly recommended.

**Recommendation for volatile alloys.** For Mg/Zn-bearing aluminium alloys, budget for sacrificial cover slides changed every 1–3 builds (more frequent for high-Mg alloys), supplement the bed cross-flow with a dedicated window gas knife, and monitor transmitted power with a photodiode on the return path of a dichroic beamsplitter.

---

## 5. Galvo Aperture Clipping, Mirror Heating, and Edge Effects

**Beam-to-aperture margin.** The SCANLAB basiCube 20 has a 20 mm entrance aperture. With a 7.5 mm collimated beam (1/e² diameter), the beam-to-aperture ratio is 20/7.5 ≈ 2.67, which provides adequate margin against clipping on the entry mirror. With a 5 mm beam, this ratio increases to 4.0, which is safer for clipping but produces a larger diffraction-limited spot (scaling inversely with beam diameter on the lens). As a conservative design rule, the worst-case clear semi-aperture at any scan angle should be ≥1.5× the 1/e² beam radius.

**Mirror heating.** The basiCube mirrors are rated for approximately 1 kW at 1064 nm without active cooling. At 500 W CW with high-quality dielectric coatings (absorption <0.1%), thermal loading on each mirror is approximately 0.5 W, which is manageable without cooling for typical scan patterns. However, long dwell times on a single mirror position (e.g., during hatch scanning near one field edge) increase local heating and may introduce transient pointing drift.

**Angle of incidence and spot ellipticity.** For a 75 mm diameter scan field with f = 160 mm, the maximum half-field scan angle is arctan(37.5/160) ≈ 13.2°. With f = 254 mm, this reduces to arctan(37.5/254) ≈ 8.4°. The geometric spot elongation from oblique incidence on the powder bed is 1/cos θ, giving 1.027× at 13.2° and 1.011× at 8.4°—modest in themselves. However, combined scanner and lens aberrations produce measurable spot elongation at field edges (pqac-00000025). The beam is approximately circular only at the build-plane centre and becomes increasingly elliptical with radial distance (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). This elongation causes position-dependent changes in effective power density and melt-pool depth: perpendicular elongation reduces penetration, while parallel elongation can partially compensate through increased interaction time (pqac-00000026). Edge-of-field positions show increased porosity and surface roughness (pqac-00000025).

**Recommendation.** Use f = 254 mm for a 75 mm field (8.4° max angle) rather than f = 160 mm (13.2°), accepting a larger nominal spot. Measure caustic, power, ellipticity, and centroid at centre, mid-axes, and corners after thermal stabilisation to build a field-correction map.

---

## 6. Commissioning Instruments and Melt-Pool Monitoring

**Beam characterisation.** NIST's open-architecture AMMT/TEMPS LPBF platform uses a 500 W fibre laser with a shared optical train supporting both high-power delivery and broadband measurement, including filtered detectors and a high-speed imager with FPGA-based real-time processing (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028). Commercial LPBF beam-characterisation tools reported in the literature include the Focus Beam Profiler (FBP), BeamWatch AM (BWAM), FocusMonitor+ (FM+), and 3-D Beam Mapper; the latter is used to map beam characteristics across the entire working envelope (pqac-00000029).

**Minimum commissioning kit:**
- **Power meter:** Calibrated thermopile or water-cooled calorimeter rated ≥600 W (e.g., Ophir 500A-BB-34 or Coherent LM-500).
- **Beam profiler / focus finder:** A system capable of measuring ≈75 µm caustics (e.g., Primes FocusMonitor, Ophir BeamWatch, or Spiricon pyroelectric array with appropriate attenuation).
- **IR viewer / detector card:** 1070 nm sensitive cards or phosphor-coated viewers for alignment.
- **Visible alignment laser:** A co-aligned HeNe or red diode for coarse optical path verification.
- **Scan-field calibration:** Engraved or anodised stainless-steel calibration plates marked at known grid positions, plus a metrology microscope or optical CMM for affine and higher-order field correction.
- **Thermal camera:** For monitoring optic temperatures during power ramp.

**Melt-pool monitoring.** Coaxial monitoring in LPBF uses a dichroic beamsplitter inserted into the laser path before the galvo scanner head: the ≈1070 nm processing beam passes through, while shorter-wavelength thermal radiation from the melt pool is reflected to sensors (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). Commercial implementations include the Renishaw AM250's dual-camera system using two Photron FASTCAM SA5 high-speed cameras with wavelength-specific bandpass filters for two-colour thermography, plus a Thorlabs PDA10C photodiode for laser power monitoring (pqac-00000015). Two-wavelength pyrometers using InGaAs photodiodes enable emissivity-independent temperature estimation (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000017).

For a basiCube-class head, the simplest fit is a fast coaxial Si or InGaAs photodiode (sensitive to thermal emission in the 900–1700 nm range) fed via a dichroic beamsplitter and laser-line notch filter, providing a scalar melt-pool intensity signal correlated with temperature and pool size. An off-axis global-view camera (visible or SWIR) adds layer-by-layer imaging capability. Full two-band coaxial pyrometry requires calibrated optics and careful field-of-view registration.

---

## 7. Laser Safety Optics

**Viewing windows for a Class 1 enclosure.** For a 1070 nm fibre laser at 500 W, viewing windows in the enclosure must attenuate any conceivable direct or scattered beam to below the Class 1 accessible emission limit (AEL). An optical density of OD 7 at 1070 nm attenuates 500 W to 50 nW, which is well below the CW Class 1 AEL at this wavelength (pqac-00000014). The required OD must be calculated per IEC 60825-1 from the specific viewing geometry, wavelength band, and exposure duration. Certified laser-safety filter glass (e.g., Laservision, Kentek, or NOIR) rated for the 1000–1100 nm band with OD ≥7 is recommended. Polycarbonate with appropriate absorptive filter dyes is another option, but glass filter windows are more resistant to surface damage and degradation.

**Guard and enclosure burn-through.** IEC 60825-4 (and ANSI Z136.1) require that protective housings withstand the maximum foreseeable laser exposure for a specified guard time. Burn-through time for 1.6 mm aluminium sheet exposed to a 500 W CW beam at 1070 nm is not a fixed number—it depends strongly on spot size (focused vs. defocused), beam intensity profile, alloy thermal conductivity, surface reflectivity, and cooling (pqac-00000042). Aluminium's high reflectivity at 1 µm (>90%) initially reflects most incident power, dramatically slowing penetration compared to steel; once absorption increases at elevated temperature, thermal conductivity rapidly conducts heat away from the spot (pqac-00000042). For a defocused beam (as would typically strike a guard panel), the irradiance may be well below the absorption-coupled melting threshold, potentially preventing penetration entirely.

**Practical guidance:** Prefer steel guards (1.5–3 mm mild steel) over aluminium for the beam enclosure, as steel has lower reflectivity and conductivity at 1 µm, providing more predictable guard behaviour. Use double-walled construction with an air gap. Install beam traps at foreseeable direct-beam impingement points. Interlock all doors, removable panels, window shutters, and monitor loss of coolant/flow and scanner faults. Commission the entire enclosure through a formal laser safety assessment per IEC 60825-1/IEC 60825-4, including a hazard analysis and, ideally, an empirical guard penetration test at maximum power with the worst-case focused beam geometry. Do not rely solely on a calculated burn-through time (pqac-00000042).

---

## Summary of Key Concerns

The proposed beam path is feasible but demands attention to several aluminium-specific risks: (1) thermal focal shift in fused-silica optics can exceed the Rayleigh range even at 500 W if surfaces become contaminated with Mg/Zn condensate—crystalline quartz or aThermoXX alternatives should be considered at minimum for the chamber window (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041); (2) catalogue marking-grade f-theta lenses lack CW thermal qualification; (3) back-reflection from aluminium mandates verified laser protection and operational protocols (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013); (4) volatile-element condensate requires a dedicated window gas knife in addition to the bed cross-flow (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045); (5) a 7.5 mm beam with f = 254 mm is preferred over f = 160 mm for edge-spot quality over a 75 mm field (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026); (6) a minimum set of beam-characterisation and monitoring tools must be budgeted from the outset (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029); and (7) laser-safety design should use steel guards, OD ≥7 viewing filters, and a formal IEC 60825 hazard analysis rather than relying on aluminium burn-through estimates."}

(7) Laser safety optics: which window materials and OD ratings for viewing windows in a Class 1 enclosure, and guard burn-through times for 1.6 mm aluminium at 500 W. ## 1. Thermal Focal Shift of Fused-Silica Optics

Fused silica has a high temperature coefficient of optical path length (TCOP, G ≈ 9.03 × 10⁻⁶/K), and its relatively low thermal conductivity (≈1.31 W/m·K) produces steep radial temperature gradients under absorbed laser power, resulting in strong negative focal shift (laskin2021ontheselection pages 22-25, laskin2022ontheselection pages 6-8). Experimentally, a contaminated (fingerprint) fused-silica focusing lens showed a focal shift of −0.32 mm at 2.5 kW and −0.47 mm at 4.5 kW, in reasonable agreement with calculated values of −0.31 and −0.40 mm respectively (laskin2022ontheselection pages 9-12). At 500 W, the absolute shift scales approximately linearly with absorbed power, but the absorbed fraction depends critically on coating quality and surface cleanliness. Faas et al. measured an intensity-specific thermal refractive power D* of 0.55 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for a new fused-silica lens with a high-quality wavelength-specific coating, versus 1.16–1.27 × 10⁻⁶ mm/W for used, uncoated fused-silica lenses (faas2018determinationofthe pages 5-7). Broadband coatings introduce substantially greater thermal power than the substrate alone (faas2018determinationofthe pages 3-5).

**Contamination effect.** Even a fingerprint or thin dust layer on a fused-silica window in a welding shop or SLM chamber creates a temperature gradient that shifts the focus and distorts the spot profile (laskin2021ontheselection pages 22-25). This is especially relevant for aluminium LPBF where Mg and Zn condensate continuously deposits on optics.

**Athermal alternatives.** Crystalline quartz (SiO₂, extraordinary orientation) has near-zero TCOP and thermo-optical ratio (TOR ≈ −0.04 × 10⁻⁶ W/m vs. 6.89 × 10⁻⁶ W/m for fused silica), fulfilling the self-compensation condition almost exactly. Sapphire achieves a low TOR (0.38–0.39 × 10⁻⁶ W/m) through extremely high thermal conductivity despite a high TCOP. The specialty glass aThermoXX (TCOP ≈ −0.31 × 10⁻⁶/K) offers near-zero thermal lensing and is used for SLM protective windows at power densities up to about 3 kW/cm² (laskin2021ontheselection pages 22-25, laskin2021ontheselection pages 25-26). Undoped YAG is another candidate for high-power windows, with good hardness and machining properties, though available sizes are typically limited to about 1 inch (laskin2021ontheselection pages 25-26).

**Detection and compensation.** LPBF builders should perform Z-scan burn tests (a staircase of single tracks at varying Z-offset) at cold start and after thermal soak to quantify the focal shift in situ. Trending delivered power and focal position before every build using an inline or removable focus monitor is essential. The relationship Δf/z_R ≈ −D* × P/(λ × M²) can be used for first-order estimation (faas2018determinationofthe pages 1-3).

---

## 2. F-Theta Lens Suitability at 500 W CW

A catalogue marking-grade f-theta lens (Thorlabs FTH series or similar) is typically specified with a pulsed laser-induced damage threshold (LIDT), which is not directly applicable to CW operation. At 500 W CW, the governing failure mode is not instantaneous optical damage but cumulative thermal degradation: coating absorption, thermal lensing, and thermally induced stress. The coating is the dominant thermal contributor—broadband coatings can produce roughly double the thermal refractive power of an uncoated substrate (faas2018determinationofthe pages 5-7, faas2018determinationofthe pages 3-5).

Fused-silica f-theta lenses have been successfully used in LPBF at 500 W with a 35 µm spot for copper processing, though this required careful attention to thermal effects (stoll2020processdevelopmentfor pages 9-13). Commercial LPBF machines (EOS, SLM Solutions, Renishaw) typically use industrial-grade fused-silica f-theta lenses from suppliers such as Sill Optics or Linos/Excelitas, which are specifically rated and warranty-qualified for CW multi-hundred-watt operation. These are generally non-telecentric designs for smaller machines, with telecentric lenses reserved for larger scan fields where constant spot size and normal incidence are critical.

**Recommendation.** Do not qualify a low-cost lens from its pulsed LIDT number alone. Require from the vendor: (a) total absorption specification at 1070 nm CW, (b) thermal focal shift data at the intended power and duty cycle, (c) clear aperture trace at all scan angles for the intended beam diameter, and (d) a warranty covering the CW operating conditions. If the vendor cannot provide this data, budget for an industrial LPBF-grade lens (Sill S4LFT or comparable).

---

## 3. Back-Reflection from Aluminium Melt Pools

Aluminium reflects approximately 90% of 1070 nm radiation from a polished bulk surface; copper can exceed 95% (naeem2013laserprocessingof pages 1-2, canacoo2026laseradditivemanufacturing pages 6-8). However, the fraction actually recoupled into the delivery fibre in LPBF is much smaller because: the melt pool is rough and displaced from the beam waist; the surface is not normal to the beam at most scan positions; and the collection solid angle of the return path through the f-theta and galvo is limited (rivera2018nextgenerationfiberlasers pages 3-5). Nevertheless, even a brief specular return during initial melting on a smooth build plate can deliver dangerous power spikes.

**Damage mechanisms.** Back-reflected light travelling through the delivery optics can overheat polymer fibre components, damage optical coatings on the galvo mirrors, and destabilise or damage the laser source (naeem2013laserprocessingof pages 3-3, canacoo2026laseradditivemanufacturing pages 6-8). Copper LPBF studies have documented optical mirror coating damage during high-power processing (stoll2020processdevelopmentfor pages 9-13).

**Protection strategies.** Several approaches are used in practice:

- **Laser internal protection:** Modern IPG YLR-series lasers include an internal back-reflection monitor and automatic power shutdown when reflected power exceeds a threshold. The YLR-500-SM likely tolerates some reflected power, but the exact specification should be obtained from IPG for the specific serial number configuration (naeem2013laserprocessingof pages 3-3).
- **Free-space isolators:** Faraday isolators provide high isolation (>30 dB) but introduce insertion loss, thermal load, and potential beam degradation; at 500 W single-mode they are expensive and require careful thermal management (naeem2013laserprocessingof pages 3-3).
- **Beam dump and monitoring:** JK Lasers/IPG developed systems that redirect back-reflected light into a beam dump and continuously monitor reflection levels, automatically shutting down the laser when limits are exceeded (naeem2013laserprocessingof pages 3-3).
- **Tilting the processing head/window:** Tilting diverts specular returns away from the fibre but produces an elliptical, larger spot with lower power density and potentially increased heat input (naeem2013laserprocessingof pages 3-3).
- **Operational protocols:** Avoid stationary exposure at the exact field centre, never fire at full power on a bare polished build plate, use a roughened or pre-coated plate surface, and begin scanning immediately upon laser turn-on (stanisz2026angulardependenceof pages 9-11).

---

## 4. Window and Cover-Slide Contamination

**Contamination sources.** Aluminium alloys containing Mg and Zn produce significant metal vapour during LPBF. This vapour condenses as fine nanoparticulate (condensate) that, together with ejected melt-pool spatter, deposits on the chamber window and sacrificial cover slide. The condensate attenuates the laser beam through both absorption and scattering, and creates local hot spots that can nucleate thermal damage on the optics (yakubov2022laserpowderbed pages 103-108, revanur2024novelscanstrategies pages 36-38).

**Effect on delivered power.** Reducing shielding gas cross-flow from 4 m/s to 2 m/s in one study decreased melt-pool cross-sectional area by 30–50%, primarily attributed to laser attenuation by the uncleared vapour plume (reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 5-6). Most vaporised condensate particles concentrate below approximately 1 mm above the keyhole, so attenuation is strongest near the interaction zone (reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 5-6).

**Gas flow requirements.** A cross-flow velocity of approximately 2.5–4.0 m/s above the powder bed effectively clears the vapour plume and bends spatter trajectories downstream (reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 4-5). Below 2.0 m/s, porosity increases exponentially and process stability degrades (reijonen2020ontheeffect pages 5-6). A modified two-row nozzle arrangement increased spatter removal efficiency from 69% to 93% (sing2020laserpowderbed pages 13-19). The proposed 2.5–3 m/s cross-flow is at the lower end of the effective range.

**Window protection design.** Patents for LPBF machines describe a dual gas-inlet architecture: a horizontal cross-flow across the bed for plume/spatter removal, plus a separate downward-flowing "gas knife" adjacent to the transmission element (window) that creates a curtain of clean gas preventing rising condensate from reaching the optics (EP3147047B1 pages 3-5, EP3321003B1 pages 4-5). Porous sintered-metal or fibre-web flow straighteners with 20–90% porosity and 1–10 mm pore sizes produce laminar flow and uniform velocity profiles (EP3321003B1 pages 4-5). Commercial practice is to clean the optical window after every build (revanur2024novelscanstrategies pages 51-53).

**Window tilting.** A slight wedge or tilt on the chamber window (1–2°) prevents ghost reflections from the window surfaces from propagating back along the beam path into the galvo and fibre. This is standard practice on many LPBF machines and highly recommended.

**Recommendation for volatile alloys.** For Mg/Zn-bearing aluminium alloys, budget for sacrificial cover slides changed every 1–3 builds (more frequent for high-Mg alloys), supplement the bed cross-flow with a dedicated window gas knife, and monitor transmitted power with a photodiode on the return path of a dichroic beamsplitter.

---

## 5. Galvo Aperture Clipping, Mirror Heating, and Edge Effects

**Beam-to-aperture margin.** The SCANLAB basiCube 20 has a 20 mm entrance aperture. With a 7.5 mm collimated beam (1/e² diameter), the beam-to-aperture ratio is 20/7.5 ≈ 2.67, which provides adequate margin against clipping on the entry mirror. With a 5 mm beam, this ratio increases to 4.0, which is safer for clipping but produces a larger diffraction-limited spot (scaling inversely with beam diameter on the lens). As a conservative design rule, the worst-case clear semi-aperture at any scan angle should be ≥1.5× the 1/e² beam radius.

**Mirror heating.** The basiCube mirrors are rated for approximately 1 kW at 1064 nm without active cooling. At 500 W CW with high-quality dielectric coatings (absorption <0.1%), thermal loading on each mirror is approximately 0.5 W, which is manageable without cooling for typical scan patterns. However, long dwell times on a single mirror position (e.g., during hatch scanning near one field edge) increase local heating and may introduce transient pointing drift.

**Angle of incidence and spot ellipticity.** For a 75 mm diameter scan field with f = 160 mm, the maximum half-field scan angle is arctan(37.5/160) ≈ 13.2°. With f = 254 mm, this reduces to arctan(37.5/254) ≈ 8.4°. The geometric spot elongation from oblique incidence on the powder bed is 1/cos θ, giving 1.027× at 13.2° and 1.011× at 8.4°—modest in themselves. However, combined scanner and lens aberrations produce measurable spot elongation at field edges (hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 74-79). The beam is approximately circular only at the build-plane centre and becomes increasingly elliptical with radial distance (hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 74-79, hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 79-84). This elongation causes position-dependent changes in effective power density and melt-pool depth: perpendicular elongation reduces penetration, while parallel elongation can partially compensate through increased interaction time (hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 79-84). Edge-of-field positions show increased porosity and surface roughness (hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 74-79).

**Recommendation.** Use f = 254 mm for a 75 mm field (8.4° max angle) rather than f = 160 mm (13.2°), accepting a larger nominal spot. Measure caustic, power, ellipticity, and centroid at centre, mid-axes, and corners after thermal stabilisation to build a field-correction map.

---

## 6. Commissioning Instruments and Melt-Pool Monitoring

**Beam characterisation.** NIST's open-architecture AMMT/TEMPS LPBF platform uses a 500 W fibre laser with a shared optical train supporting both high-power delivery and broadband measurement, including filtered detectors and a high-speed imager with FPGA-based real-time processing (grantham2016opticaldesignand pages 2-4, grantham2016opticaldesignand pages 1-2). Commercial LPBF beam-characterisation tools reported in the literature include the Focus Beam Profiler (FBP), BeamWatch AM (BWAM), FocusMonitor+ (FM+), and 3-D Beam Mapper; the latter is used to map beam characteristics across the entire working envelope (hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 15-21).

**Minimum commissioning kit:**
- **Power meter:** Calibrated thermopile or water-cooled calorimeter rated ≥600 W (e.g., Ophir 500A-BB-34 or Coherent LM-500).
- **Beam profiler / focus finder:** A system capable of measuring ≈75 µm caustics (e.g., Primes FocusMonitor, Ophir BeamWatch, or Spiricon pyroelectric array with appropriate attenuation).
- **IR viewer / detector card:** 1070 nm sensitive cards or phosphor-coated viewers for alignment.
- **Visible alignment laser:** A co-aligned HeNe or red diode for coarse optical path verification.
- **Scan-field calibration:** Engraved or anodised stainless-steel calibration plates marked at known grid positions, plus a metrology microscope or optical CMM for affine and higher-order field correction.
- **Thermal camera:** For monitoring optic temperatures during power ramp.

**Melt-pool monitoring.** Coaxial monitoring in LPBF uses a dichroic beamsplitter inserted into the laser path before the galvo scanner head: the ≈1070 nm processing beam passes through, while shorter-wavelength thermal radiation from the melt pool is reflected to sensors (hooper2018meltpooltemperature pages 4-6, fox2024inprocessmonitoringand pages 44-47). Commercial implementations include the Renishaw AM250's dual-camera system using two Photron FASTCAM SA5 high-speed cameras with wavelength-specific bandpass filters for two-colour thermography, plus a Thorlabs PDA10C photodiode for laser power monitoring (hooper2018meltpooltemperature pages 4-6). Two-wavelength pyrometers using InGaAs photodiodes enable emissivity-independent temperature estimation (sun2019computationalfluiddynamics pages 53-56, lafirenza2025developmentofinsitu pages 35-37).

For a basiCube-class head, the simplest fit is a fast coaxial Si or InGaAs photodiode (sensitive to thermal emission in the 900–1700 nm range) fed via a dichroic beamsplitter and laser-line notch filter, providing a scalar melt-pool intensity signal correlated with temperature and pool size. An off-axis global-view camera (visible or SWIR) adds layer-by-layer imaging capability. Full two-band coaxial pyrometry requires calibrated optics and careful field-of-view registration.

---

## 7. Laser Safety Optics

**Viewing windows for a Class 1 enclosure.** For a 1070 nm fibre laser at 500 W, viewing windows in the enclosure must attenuate any conceivable direct or scattered beam to below the Class 1 accessible emission limit (AEL). An optical density of OD 7 at 1070 nm attenuates 500 W to 50 nW, which is well below the CW Class 1 AEL at this wavelength (stanisz2026angulardependenceof pages 9-11). The required OD must be calculated per IEC 60825-1 from the specific viewing geometry, wavelength band, and exposure duration. Certified laser-safety filter glass (e.g., Laservision, Kentek, or NOIR) rated for the 1000–1100 nm band with OD ≥7 is recommended. Polycarbonate with appropriate absorptive filter dyes is another option, but glass filter windows are more resistant to surface damage and degradation.

**Guard and enclosure burn-through.** IEC 60825-4 (and ANSI Z136.1) require that protective housings withstand the maximum foreseeable laser exposure for a specified guard time. Burn-through time for 1.6 mm aluminium sheet exposed to a 500 W CW beam at 1070 nm is not a fixed number—it depends strongly on spot size (focused vs. defocused), beam intensity profile, alloy thermal conductivity, surface reflectivity, and cooling (ozgoren2011highpowerallfiber pages 65-70). Aluminium's high reflectivity at 1 µm (>90%) initially reflects most incident power, dramatically slowing penetration compared to steel; once absorption increases at elevated temperature, thermal conductivity rapidly conducts heat away from the spot (ozgoren2011highpowerallfiber pages 65-70). For a defocused beam (as would typically strike a guard panel), the irradiance may be well below the absorption-coupled melting threshold, potentially preventing penetration entirely.

**Practical guidance:** Prefer steel guards (1.5–3 mm mild steel) over aluminium for the beam enclosure, as steel has lower reflectivity and conductivity at 1 µm, providing more predictable guard behaviour. Use double-walled construction with an air gap. Install beam traps at foreseeable direct-beam impingement points. Interlock all doors, removable panels, window shutters, and monitor loss of coolant/flow and scanner faults. Commission the entire enclosure through a formal laser safety assessment per IEC 60825-1/IEC 60825-4, including a hazard analysis and, ideally, an empirical guard penetration test at maximum power with the worst-case focused beam geometry. Do not rely solely on a calculated burn-through time (ozgoren2011highpowerallfiber pages 65-70).

---

## Summary of Key Concerns

The proposed beam path is feasible but demands attention to several aluminium-specific risks: (1) thermal focal shift in fused-silica optics can exceed the Rayleigh range even at 500 W if surfaces become contaminated with Mg/Zn condensate—crystalline quartz or aThermoXX alternatives should be considered at minimum for the chamber window (laskin2021ontheselection pages 22-25, laskin2021ontheselection pages 25-26); (2) catalogue marking-grade f-theta lenses lack CW thermal qualification; (3) back-reflection from aluminium mandates verified laser protection and operational protocols (naeem2013laserprocessingof pages 3-3); (4) volatile-element condensate requires a dedicated window gas knife in addition to the bed cross-flow (EP3321003B1 pages 4-5, EP3147047B1 pages 3-5); (5) a 7.5 mm beam with f = 254 mm is preferred over f = 160 mm for edge-spot quality over a 75 mm field (hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 74-79, hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 79-84); (6) a minimum set of beam-characterisation and monitoring tools must be budgeted from the outset (grantham2016opticaldesignand pages 2-4, hernandez2023designandimplementation pages 15-21); and (7) laser-safety design should use steel guards, OD ≥7 viewing filters, and a formal IEC 60825 hazard analysis rather than relying on aluminium burn-through estimates.
